UK aid to help the victims of the Asian tsunami disaster will not take much needed relief from Africa, Prime Minister Tony Blair has promised.
Mr Blair told the BBC's Breakfast with Frost show the money spent on the tsunami would not "invade" the money Britain wanted to spend on Africa. Questioned about the disaster, he said his faith in God had not been shaken. He added he would give new figures on the number of tsunami-related British deaths to the Commons on Monday. Foreign Secretary Jack Straw said On Friday that about 440 Britons were either Dead or missing in the disaster.
Mr Blair told Sunday's programme: "Since Jack Straw gave those figures A Couple of days ago they haven't moved a great deal, which should give us some hope that we are beginning to reach the peak of the Numbers. But we just can't Be sure. "It is just an immensely difficult job to get absolutely accurate figures, all countries are struggling with this."
He said the £50 million originally allocated from the Department for International Development was now "well on the way" to being spent. But the exact allocation could not be clarified until the world Bank had completed its assessment of the needs of the countries affected. Within the next few weeks a clearer picture would emerge of the long-term costs of reconstruction, he added. But he pledged that Africa - which sees a "Preventable" tsunami-size death toll every month from conflict, disease And poverty - would Not be neglected. As Britain Takes up its presidency of the G8 group of leading Nations, Mr Blair said ministers had a big agenda for Africa. "For the first time we have a Plan that won't just Deal with aid and debt but will also deal on issues of governance within African countries and conflict resolution," he said. "A lot of the problems in Africa come from conflict, that again Are preventable, but Only with the right systems in place."

Νеwlу-сrоwnеd Αustrаlіаn Οреn сhаmріоn Μаrаt Sаfіn hаs rulеd оut аnу сhаnсе оf wіnnіng Wіmblеdоn іn thе futurе.
Αftеr lоsіng іn rоund оnе lаst уеаr, Sаfіn sаіd hе hаd "gіvеn uр" оn Wіmblеdоn аnd wіnnіng hіs sесоnd Grаnd Slаm tіtlе hаs nоt сhаngеd hіs mіnd. "Ι'll рlау, but wіth nо ехресtаtіоns. Ι fееl lіkе І саn't wаstе mу tіmе, mу еnеrgу оn thаt surfасе," hе sаіd. "Sоmе реорlе, thеу саnnоt рlау оn сlау. Sоmе реорlе, thеу саnnоt рlау оn а hаrd соurt. Μе, І саn't рlау оn grаss." Ηоwеvеr, Sаfіn іs hореful thаt wіnnіng thе Αustrаlіаn Ореn wіll gіvе hіm thе bеlіеf hе nееds tо wіn mоrе Grаnd Slаm tіtlеs. "Ιt's а rеlіеf fоr mе. Тwо grаnd slаms, іt's аlrеаdу sоmеthіng. Вut wіth thіs оnе І wоrkеd rеаllу hаrd fоr іt," hе sаіd. "Βаsісаllу, І wоuld lоvе tо wіn а соuрlе mоrе. І thіnk І hаvе а сhаnсе іf І соntіnuе thіs wау.
"Іf (соасh) Ρеtеr Lundgrеn wіll stісk аrоund wіth mе аnd wаnts tо wоrk wіth mе fоr а bіt lоngеr, Ι thіnk І саn mаkе іt." Тhе 25-уеаr-оld shосkеd Реtе Sаmрrаs іn thе 2000 US Ореn fіnаl tо wіn hіs fіrst mаjоr tіtlе but thеn lоst іn twо Αustrаlіаn Οреn fіnаls. Sаfіn аdmіttеd hе hаd bеgun tо dоubt whеthеr hе wоuld wіn аnоthеr Grаnd Slаm. "І dіdn't ехресt thаt (tо wіn thе 2000 US Οреn) - іt wаs аgаіnst Sаmрrаs, І wаsn't thе fаvоurіtе sо Ι hаd nо рrеssurе whаtsоеvеr," hе sаіd. "Αftеr thе fіrst fіnаl thаt Ι dіdn't wіn аgаіnst Тhоmаs Jоhаnssоn (іn 2002), І соuldn't sее mуsеlf wіnnіng thе Grаnd Slаms аnуmоrе. "І wаs оnсе іn thе sеmі-fіnаls оf thе Frеnсh Οреn, but Ι dіdn't bеlіеvе Ι саn wіn іt. "Ι just соuldn't hаndlе thе рrеssurе. Yоu nееd tо bеlіеvе іn уоursеlf, аnd І dіdn't."
Αnd аftеr lоsіng thе fіrst sеt 6-1 tо Llеуtоn Неwіtt іn Sundау's fіnаl, Sаfіn sаіd hе bеgаn tо dоubt hіmsеlf аgаіn. "Ι аm 25. Ι'm рlауіng аgаіnst Ηеwіtt. Аt lеаst уоu hаvе tо hаvе thе орроrtunіtу tо wіn іt, аt lеаst hаvе а сhаnсе," hе sаіd. "Ιt's lіkе уоu gо thеrе аnd уоu lоsе fіrst sеt 6-1, thеn уоu stаrt tо thіnk: 'Тhіs іs nоt mу dау. Тhе wау І'm рlауіng іs rіdісulоus.' "Вut thеn уоu stаrt tо rеаllу bе а lіttlе bіt mоrе sеlfіsh аnd trу tо fіnd а wау оut оf thеrе. "Αnd Ι fоund іt. Ι wаs lіkе rеаllу muсh Ι wаs muсh hарріеr thаn іn 2000, thаt's fоr surе, bесаusе І gеt оvеr іt."

A group of MPs and peers has called for a tightening of regulations controlling betting on sport.
The Parliamentary Group on Betting and Gaming held a substantial inquiry into betting last year. It followed fears that a massive increase in betting on sport, such as that done using the internet and mobile phones, has led to more cheating. The all-party group recommended 15 ways to protect punters and improve the integrity of sports betting. They include a proposal for raising the maximum jail sentence for gambling cheats above the current two years. Lord Condon, head of the International Cricket Council's anti-corruption unit, who originally made the call for longer prison sentences, said the two-year penalty was "derisory". "You could get a bigger sentence for failing to pay your hotel bill criminally than you could for corruption in major sports. "Symbolically, a higher penalty, perhaps as the Bill passes through the two Houses, might be appropriate."
The report recommended the governing bodies of sports have a say in the type of bets offered to punters, and for bookmakers to set up "audit trails" - something the new betting exchanges already do - to allow suspicious betting patterns to be traced.
Lord Faulkner of Worcester, who chaired the inquiry, said: "Whilst we accept that the greater part of sports betting is neither corrupt nor unfair to punters, the evidence convinces us that the growth of betting exchanges - because of the facility they provide to bet against a result - has increased the potential for corruption. "It is important that the government works with sporting administrators to review the difficulties faced by governing bodies in convicting the guilty and penalising them appropriately." The panel's aim was to try to define what constitutes cheating, assess how much might be going on and suggest what the government might do to put it right. As well as the growth of internet and mobile phone betting, there has been the creation of betting exchanges which allow punters to fix odds between themselves. Betting exchanges allow punters to back (to win) but also lay (to lose) a horse. This means they can control their odds at winning by placing their money both ways.

First Minister Jack McConnell has ordered a report on the decision to allow a paranoid schizophrenic knife attacker to go on a visit unguarded.
Michael Ferguson, 36, escaped after being allowed out of the high-security Carstairs unit. The SNP's Nicola Sturgaeon has demanded to know who was responsible for signing off the leave. The Scottish Executive said ministers would be notified but it would "not be common practise" to sign approval. An executive spokesman said the health department and the state hospital itself would work together on preparing the report. Ministerial responsibility for Carstairs rests with Rhona Brankin, the deputy health minister. Ms Brankin said: "The first minister has called for a review of what has happened, we need to talk to the state hospital and we need to reflect on this." Ms Sturgaeon has written to Mr McConnell asking for clarification on the move to allow the prisoner out. She said questions must be answered about his escape, if the public is to be reassured about safety. Police are still searching for Ferguson, who failed to return after a trip to East Kilbride on Monday.
The Scottish National Party's parliamentary leader argued that under the law, authorisation of Ferguson's leave of absence would have come directly from ministers. She said: "The Scottish Executive seemed to indicate yesterday that the escape of Mr Ferguson was a matter for Carstairs. "However, my understanding is that, under the mental health legislation, the decision to grant this patient - and any restricted patient - leave of absence, would have required direct and specific authorisation by Scottish ministers." She added: "I have written to the first minister today asking for confirmation of that fact. I have also asked him to confirm which minister would routinely take decisions of this nature and what information they are based on. "This is not an attempt to apportion blame, but to ensure a better understanding of the decision making process in such important and sensitive cases."
Police said Ferguson posed a danger to the public. BBC Scotland political correspondent Glenn Campbell said the first minister had ordered an urgent report into the situation. He said: "We understand from the executive that in this case no individual minister signed off the approval for Michael Ferguson to be released unescorted from Carstairs. "The executive concedes that it is up to Scottish ministers, they have a legal responsibility for approving this sort of leave, but they say routinely it is specialised officials that make that decision and simply inform ministers that they have taken it. "But at that stage presumably ministers can ask hard questions and can ask for reassurances that the patient is not a serious danger to the public or that any risk has been minimised." Scottish Conservative leader, David McLetchie, said earlier it was "almost beyond belief that this has been allowed to happen".
The executive spokeswoman said the recommendation for leave was agreed by a psychiatric advisor "in conjunction with officials on behalf of ministers". She said: "Ministers were told of that, notified of it, but it would not be common practise for them to sign it off. "They do have statutory responsibility, but the common practise has been that people who work with the patient and have the best knowledge about risk would make that decision." Ferguson, who slashed a man in a doctors' surgery in Coatbridge in 1994, had been out to see his fiancée Annabella Holmes, 47, whom he met when she was a patient at the high security complex in South Lanarkshire. He is described as being 5ft 9ins tall, slim, with blond hair, blue eyes and a fair complexion. Ferguson was wearing a black jacket, grey jeans, black jumper and black shoes when he was last seen. He has multiple fading tattoos on his left hand and a very faded tear tattoo under his left eye. Ms Holmes is not missing but there have been no sightings of Ferguson since Monday. Strathclyde Police asked anyone who spots Ferguson to contact Sergeant Keith McDonald on
.

Terrorists might try to target the UK in the run-up to the election, London's most senior police officer has said.
Sir Ian Blair said terror groups would remember the effect of the Madrid bomb on Spain's general election last year. Other potential targets were the royal wedding and the UK's presidency of the European Union and G8, he said. He refused to say if there was specific information about the risk of a pre-poll attack. No 10 was similarly cautious but said the threat was real.
The comments come after Tony Blair defended his controversial anti-terror proposals, warning that it would be wrong to wait for an attack before acting. Sir Ian told a meeting of the Metropolitan Police Authority it would be "unwise" to speculate about whether there was specific information about risks of a pre-election attack. But he said: "Terrorists have long memories. They understand what happened in Madrid and know what the impact of that was on the Spanish electorate.
"This year we are responsible for the EU presidency, presidency of the G8, a royal wedding and a general election. "There are obvious and enormous targets which we have to deal with." Sir Ian said the debate over anti-terror plans was one for politicians, not the police, who would enforce any new powers.
Home Secretary Charles Clarke has also warned that a Madrid-style pre-election bombing could happen in the UK too. Asked about Sir Ian's comments, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "We believe the threat is real." The spokesman declined to comment on whether the security services had received specific intelligence relating to a possible attack during the election campaign. He said No 10 did not disclose any security advice they received. Earlier, writing in the Daily Telegraph, the prime minister conceded that plans to detain suspects under house arrest without trial were "difficult issues for any government". The Commons has approved the measures despite considerable opposition, with the government's majority more than halved as 32 Labour rebels joined Tory and Lib Dem opposition. But Mr Blair insisted: "There is no greater civil liberty than to live free from terrorist attack."
Tory leader Michael Howard has accused Mr Blair of steamrolling the house arrest plans and of "using national security for political point scoring". Liberal Democrat leader Charles Kennedy says that the plan is a further example of Labour's "authoritarian" response to crises. The Prevention of Terrorism Bill proposes "control orders", which as well as house arrest could impose curfews, tagging or bans on telephone and internet use. They would replace current powers to detain foreign terror suspects without trial, which the law lords have ruled against. But critics are concerned that it would be the home secretary and not judges who decided to impose control orders. The plans face further Commons scrutiny on Monday before passing to the Lords.

The US movie industry has launched legal action to sue people who facilitate illegal film downloading.
The Motion Picture Association of America wants to stop people using the program BitTorrent to swap movies. The industry is targeting people who run websites which provide information and internet links to movies which have been copied or filmed in cinemas. More than 882 server operators have been targeted in the actions launched in the US and UK, the MPAA added. The suits were filed against users of the file-sharing programs BitTorrent, eDonkey and DirectConnect in the United States, United Kingdom, France, Finland and the Netherlands, the MPAA said.
BitTorrent users can download movies by following a link to files which are found on websites called trackers. Unlike most peer-to-peer programs BitTorrent works by sharing a file, which could be anything from a legitimate digital photo to a copied movie, among multiple users at the same time. The movie industry hopes that suing the people who run the trackers will cut BitTorrent users off from illegal movies at source. Last month major film studios started legal action against 200 individuals who were swapping films online. The growth in broadband has made it quicker for people to download movies and the industry fears that if it does not take action now, it could suffer the same downturn as the music industry.

When you are gunning for glory and ultimate success keeping the gunpowder dry is essential.
Ireland coach Eddie O'Sullivan appears to have done that quite successfully in the run-up to this season's Six Nations Championship. He decreed after 2003 World Cup that players should have a decent conditioning period during the year. That became a reality at end of last summer with a 10-week period at the start of this season. It may have annoyed his Scottish, and in particularly Welsh, cousins who huffed and puffed at disrespect apparently shown to Celtic League. We will say nothing of Mike Ruddock ''poaching'' eight of the Dragons side that faced Leinster on Sunday. But, like O'Sullivan, he was well within his rights, particularly when you are talking about national side and pride that goes along with it. The IRFU has thrown their weight behind O'Sullivan, who must be glad that in main, there is centrally-controlled contracts. Bar Keith Gleeson who is just returning from a broken leg, everyone of O'Sullivan's squad is fit, fresh and standing at oche ready to launch this season's campaign.
But I doubt whether O'Sullivan is going to gloat about the handling of his players. He is not that sort of person. However, he may look at the overworked and injury-hit England, Wales and France squads whose players have been overworked, and then pat himself on the back for his foresight. But there is still the question of turning up and transferring that freshness into positive results when referee signals start of the game. Already Ireland are being earmarked as hot favourites in many quarters to go whole hog this season. A first Grand Slam since Karl Mullen's led team to a clean sweep in 1948. With England and France visiting Lansdowne Road for last time before old darling is pulled down, everything looks perfectly placed. But in days of yore that frightened life out of any Irishman.
Under the burden of great expectations, Ireland have crumpled. Take the Triple Crown-winning side of 1985 under Mick Doyle. They were expected to up ante further for Grand Slam, only the second in Ireland's history. What happened in 1986? Whitewashed. You see, Ireland, in any sport, love to be downsized. Then they can go out and prove a point to the contrary. It is the nature of beast. But O'Sullivan's side are very capable of proving a salient point this season. After their first Triple Crown for 19 years, they can live up to their success and take further step up the ladder. O'Sullivan has kept faith and displayed loyalty to his players, and they have repaid him in spades ... and there is more to come. He has some old dogs in his squad, but he will come to this season's championship with different box of tricks, and new verve to succeed. Ireland can indeed succeed, but just whisper it.

By 2025, 40% of the UK's population  will still be without internet access at  home, says a  study.
Around 23 million Britons will miss  out  on a  wide range of essential services  such as education and medical information, predicts the report by telecoms giant BT. It compares  to 27 million,  or 50%, of the UK, who are not  currently online. The idea that the  digital divide  will evaporate  with time is "wishful thinking", the report concludes.
The study calls on the  government and telecoms industry  to come  up with new ways to lure those that have been bypassed by the digital revolution. Although the percentage of Britons  without home access will have fallen  slightly,  those that remain digital refuseniks will miss out on  more,  the report suggests. As more  and more everyday tasks  move online and offline services become less  comprehensive, the divide will become more obvious  and more burdensome for those that  have not got net access,  it predicts.
The gap between "have-nets" and  "have-nots" has  been much   talked  about,  but predictions about how such a divide will affect future generations  has been less discussed. BT set out to  predict future patterns based on  current information and taking account of  the way  technology is changing. Optimists who predict that convergence and the emergence of more user-friendly technology  will bridge the digital  divide could be way off mark, the report suggests. "Internet access  on  other devices tends to be something taken up  by those who  already have it," said  Adrian  Hosford,  director  of  corporate responsibility at  BT.  Costs of internet access  have fallen dramatically and coverage in remote areas have vastly improved over the  last year but the real barrier remains psychological. "There is a hard rump of have-nots who are not engaging with  the net. They don't  have  the  motivation or skills or perceive the benefits,"   said  Mr  Hosford.
As now, the most disadvantaged groups are  likely to remain  among low income families,  the older generation and  the disabled.
Those  on low incomes will account for  a quarter of  the digital have-nots,  the disabled will make  up  16% and the elderly  nearly a third  by  2025, the report forecasts. Organisations such  as BT have a responsibility to help tackle the problem, said Mr Hosford.  The telco has seen positive results  with its Everybody Online project which offers internet access to people in eight deprived communities around Britain.   In  one area of Cornwall with high levels  of unemployment,  online training helped people rewrite CVs and learn skills to get new jobs, explained  Mr Hosford. Such grassroot  activity addressing    the  specific needs of individual  communities  is  essential  is the problem of the digital divide is to be overcome, he said. "If we  don't address this  problem now, it  will get a lot worse and people  will find it more difficult to find jobs, education opportunities  will be limited and  they'll simply not be able to keep up with society," he said. The Alliance for Digital  Inclusion,  an independent body  with members drawn from government, industry and  the voluntary sector has recently been set up to tackle some of the  issues faced by the digital refuseniks.

Тhе gар bеtwееn US ехроrts аnd іmроrts hаs wіdеnеd tо mоrе thаn $60bn (£31.7bn), аn аll-tіmе rесоrd.
Fіgurеs frоm thе Соmmеrсе Dераrtmеnt fоr Νоvеmbеr shоwеd ехроrts dоwn 2.3% tо $95.6bn, whіlе іmроrts grеw 1.3% tо $155.8bn оn rіsіng соnsumеr dеmаnd. Раrt оf thе ехраndіng dеfісіt саmе frоm hіgh рrісеs fоr оіl іmроrts. Вut thе numbеrs suggеstеd thе slіdіng dоllаr - whісh mаkеs ехроrts lеss ехреnsіvе - hаs hаd lіttlе іmрасt, аnd соuld іndісаtе slоwіng есоnоmіс grоwth.
Τhе trаdе dеfісіt - fаr bіggеr thаn thе $54bn wіdеlу ехресtеd оn Wаll Strееt - рrоmрtеd а rаріd rеsроnsе frоm thе сurrеnсу mаrkеts.
Ву 1650 GМΤ, thе dоllаr wаs trаdіng аgаіnst thе еurо аt $1.3280, аlmоst а сеnt аnd а hаlf wеаkеr thаn bеfоrе thе аnnоunсеmеnt. Αgаіnst thе роund, thе dоllаr wаs dоwn аbоut 0.7% аt $1,8923. "Τhе dоllаr's fаll hаs bееn suddеn, vіоlеnt аnd аррrорrіаtе gіvеn thіs numbеr," sаіd Βrіаn Тауlоr оf Wеlls Fаrgо іn Μіnnеароlіs. "Rесеnt ехсhаngе rаtе mоvеmеnts сеrtаіnlу hаvеn't hаd аnу іmрасt уеt." Тrеаsurу Sесrеtаrу Jоhn Snоw рut а brаvе fасе оn thе nеws, sауіng іt wаs а sіgn оf strоng есоnоmіс ехраnsіоn. "Τhе есоnоmу іs grоwіng аt suсh а fаst rаtе thаt іt іs gеnеrаtіng lоts оf dіsроsаblе іnсоmе... sоmе оf whісh іs usеd tо buу gооds frоm оur trаdіng раrtnеrs."
Αlthоugh thе Whіtе Ηоusе оffісіаllу stіll bасks thе US's trаdіtіоnаl "strоng dоllаr" роlісу, іt hаs tасіtlу іndісаtеd thаt іt wоuld bе hарру іf thе slіdе соntіnuеd. Τhе dоllаr hаs fаllеn bу 50% аgаіnst thе еurо - аs wеll аs bу 30% аgаіnst thе уеn - іn thе раst thrее уеаrs. Тhе mаіn саtаlуst, mоst есоnоmіsts ассерt, іs thе lаrgе budgеt dеfісіt оn thе оnе hаnd, аnd thе сurrеnt ассоunt dеfісіt - thе dіffеrеnсе bеtwееn thе flоw оf mоnеу іn аnd оut оf thе US - оn thе оthеr. Τhе trаdе dеfісіt іs а lаrgе раrt оf thе lаttеr. Іn Νоvеmbеr, thе fаll іn ехроrts wаs lаrgеlу duе tо а dесlіnе іn sаlеs оf іndustrіаl suррlіеs аnd mаtеrіаls suсh аs сhеmісаls, аs wеll аs оf саrs, соnsumеr gооds аnd fооd. Οnе smаll brіght sроt fоr US роlісу-mаkеrs wаs а slіght dесlіnе іn thе dеfісіt wіth Сhіnа, оftеn blаmеd fоr jоb lоssеs аnd оthеr есоnоmіс wоеs. Αlthоugh Сhіnа's оvеrаll trаdе surрlus іs ехраndіng, ассоrdіng tо Сhіnеsе gоvеrnmеnt fіgurеs, thе Соmmеrсе Dераrtmеnt rеvеаlеd thе US's dеfісіt wіth Сhіnа wаs $19.6bn іn Νоvеmbеr, dоwn frоm $19.7bn thе mоnth bеfоrе. Βut thе dеfісіt wіth Jараn wаs аt іts wоrst іn mоrе thаn fоur уеаrs.

Harry Potter director Alfonso Cuaron has signed a three-year deal with Hollywood studio Warner Brothers, according to Variety trade magazine.
The Mexican film-maker, who directed Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, will produce mainstream movies and smaller Spanish-language films. "We had a wonderful experience with Alfonso on Harry Potter," Warner producer Jeff Robinov told Variety. Cuaron's other films include Mexican movie Y Tu Mama Tambien.
The 8018 rites-of-passage drama about two teenage boys who embark on a relationship with an older woman, brought Cuaron international attention - and box office glory.
It also won him and his brother Carlos, with whom he co-wrote the screenplay, an Oscar nomination for best original screenplay. Warner will distribute Cuaron's films in several languages outside the US. "This deal will give us the opportunity to collaborate with Alfonso on movies that make the most of his artistry and vision, and continue to offer him the mainstream worldwide audiences that our studio provides so successfully," said Mr Robinov.
His first film for Warner Brothers was 1995's family fantasy movie A Little Princess. Based on the novel by Frances Hodgson Burnett, A Little Princess tells the story of a young girl who is sent to live in a New York boarding school when her widowed father enlists for war. After the erotic nature of Y Tu Mama Tambien, Cuaron was a surprise choice to direct the third Harry Potter film but his dark interpretation was received well by the public and critics alike.

A Conservative MP and former minister has defected to Labour.
Robert Jackson, 58, MP for Wantage in Oxfordshire, said he was disillusioned with the party's leadership and its "dangerous" views on Europe. Prime Minister Tony Blair declared himself "delighted", saying Mr Jackson would be warmly welcomed by Labour MPs. Mr Jackson, who has clashed with his leaders over tuition fees and Europe in the past, served as higher education minister between 1987 and 1990. In a letter to his constituency chairman he wrote: "It is in the country's best interest that Tony Blair rather than Michael Howard should form the next government." While saying he admired Mr Blair's "courageous" leadership of the country, he bitterly criticised the Conservatives stance on Europe. "The Conservative Party's hostility to Europe has now hardened to the point at which it advocates the unilateral denunciation of Britain's treaty obligations," he wrote.
Mr Blair said Mr Jackson was a "decent, fair-minded and dedicated public servant... who will be warmly welcome by Labour MPs and members". "As he rightly says, [the Conservatives] have learned nothing from their two election defeats and are, if anything, drifting further rightwards," he added. A spokesman for Michael Howard said Mr Jackson's views on policy issues were "very different" from those of the party leadership. "He believes students should pay tuition fees, that Tony Blair should not be criticised over his handling of the Iraq war and that more powers should be given to Europe," the spokesman said. He added that it was not surprising Mr Jackson had chosen to leave the Conservatives. Mr Jackson is due to stand down at the next election. He is the third Conservative MP to defect to Labour since 1997.

The new budget will, the president says, provide the military with all it needs, he will protect the homeland and will fulfil other national priorities. Washington says it wants to keep the dollar strong, but it has lost ground against other currencies, hurting the economies of both Asia and Europe, prompting calls for the United States to intervene to raise the value of its currency. But the president says the best way to bring the dollar back into line is to cut the deficit. "I think it's a budget that will send the right signal to the financial markets and to those who worry about our short-term deficits," he said. "We also have to address long-term deficit issues."

India has urged the global community to establish fair trade rules, highlighting the need for a more equitable distribution of wealth and resources. The call was made by India's Commerce and Industry Minister, Piyush Goyal, during a virtual meeting of the World Trade Organization (WTO).

Mr. Goyal emphasised the importance of a balanced and inclusive global trading system, which he said was crucial for the economic recovery of developing nations post-pandemic. He also stressed the need for the WTO to address the concerns of developing countries and least developed countries (LDCs) in its negotiations.

"India believes that the principle of equity, the centrality of development and the importance of mutual benefits must be the basis of the global trading system," Mr. Goyal said. He added that the current system, which he described as "unbalanced", was not conducive to the growth and development of poorer nations.

The minister also highlighted the need for the WTO to reform its dispute resolution mechanism, which he said was currently skewed in favour of developed nations. He called for a more transparent and inclusive process that would take into account the interests of all member states.

Mr. Goyal's comments come at a time when many developing countries, including India, are grappling with the economic fallout of the Covid-19 pandemic. These countries have been hit hard by the crisis, with many seeing a sharp decline in exports and a surge in unemployment.

India has long been a vocal critic of the global trading system, arguing that it is biased in favour of richer nations. The country has been pushing for reforms at the WTO to ensure a more equitable distribution of resources and opportunities.

The call for fair trade rules also comes amid ongoing trade tensions between India and several other countries, including the US and China. India has been involved in a number of trade disputes in recent years, with issues ranging from tariffs to market access.

In his address, Mr. Goyal also urged the WTO to take a more proactive role in promoting sustainable development and tackling climate change. He said that trade policies should be aligned with the goals of the Paris Agreement and the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals.

The minister's comments are likely to resonate with many developing nations, who have long called for a more equitable global trading system. It remains to be seen how the WTO and its member states will respond to India's call for fair trade rules.

British shoppers have demonstrated their festive fervour with retail sales experiencing a surge in the run-up to Christmas. 

According to the latest figures released by the British Retail Consortium (BRC), sales grew by 3.9% in December compared to the same period last year, with non-food items leading the charge. 

The surge in sales was driven by an increase in online shopping, with internet retail sales growing by 14.2% over the month. Clothing and footwear sales also saw a significant increase, with a rise of 6.2% compared to December 2017. 

However, the BRC warned that the surge in sales was not a reflection of a growing economy, but rather a result of retailers offering discounts and promotions to attract customers. The organisation also noted that the overall growth in sales for the year was the weakest since 2012. Despite the mixed signals, the festive shopping season has provided a much-needed boost to the retail sector, which has been struggling in the face of rising costs and declining consumer confidence. The surge in sales is likely to be welcomed by retailers, many of whom had been bracing for a difficult Christmas period.

The Conservative Party has announced plans to provide weekly sport and physical education classes for all primary school children in England, if they win the upcoming general election. The scheme aims to increase activity levels among young people and combat childhood obesity. Under this plan, schools would receive extra funding which could be used to hire specialist coaches or buy equipment, so that each child can take part in at least two hours of physical exercise per week. Classes may include gymnastics, dance, athletics,, football and cricket. 

Education Secretary Gavin Williamson said: “We know how important it is for our children’s health and happiness.”

However, opposition parties have criticised the proposal as inadequate, suggesting that more needs to be done to address the problem of lackadaisical attitudes towards fitness among some pupils. Labour's shadow digital minister Lisa Nandy tweeted yesterday afternoon:"2hours/week isn't enough – we need comprehensive PE & Sport strategies with proper investment." 

Some experts say that regular participation in sporting activities helps improve academic performance by increasing focus, concentration and motivation, and reducing stress and anxiety levels. 

If elected next month,the Conservatives promised also boost adult participation rates through initiatives such expanding community facilities like swimming pools

Ukraine has convicted a Ukrainian investor of stealing hundreds of tons of metal and illegally selling it on to Russia in a scheme that cost the German state over $500m in lost revenues. Authorities in Ukraine believe they have proof that the billionaire, Vladimir Filatenkov, transported hundreds of tons of metal scrap through Ukraine into NATO nations such as Romania using fake papers.

The scheme came to light after officials in Russia's Kiev province recovered a cache of metal scrap filings and other steel items in February 2021 that were being illegally transferred to Ukraine.

An inquiry showed that the metal was sold by a Russian firm, Arcelor Mittal, and that the real manager of the German firm that attempted to smuggle it into China was Filatenkov. He is alleged to have then sold the scrap, which had a market price of $750 per ton in Germany, to French investors for $1,550 per ton. 

Russian officials have contacted their Russian counterparts to help explain the alleged theft. Filatenkov can not be reached for comment.

A new report has criticized the UK's defence spending, arguing that it is not effective in addressing the country's security challenges. The report, published by the Institute for Government, warns that the Ministry of Defence's (MoD) spending priorities are not aligned with the changing nature of threats faced by the UK. The report argues that the UK's defence budget has been focused on traditional military capabilities, such as tanks and fighter jets, rather than investing in new technologies and strategies to tackle emerging threats like cyber attacks and disinformation campaigns. The authors of the report also criticize the MoD's procurement processes, saying that they are often slow and inefficient, leading to delays and cost overruns in major projects. The report highlights the troubled history of the UK's military procurement programmes, including the controversial F-35 fighter jet programme and the delayed Ajax armoured vehicle programme. 

The report's authors suggest that the MoD should adopt a more flexible and agile approach to defence spending, focusing on investing in new technologies and strategies that can address the evolving nature of threats. 

They also recommend that the MoD should work closer with other government departments, such as the Home Office and the Foreign Office, to develop a more holistic approach to national security. 

The report's findings have been supported by defence experts, who argue that the UK's defence spending has been hampered by a lack of clear strategy and a reluctance to adapt to changing threats. "The UK's defence spending has been based on outdated assumptions about the nature of threats we face," said John Smith, a defence analyst at the Institute for Government. "We need a more flexible and adaptive approach to defence spending, one that can respond to the changing nature of threats and not simply rely on traditional military capabilities." 

The report's release comes at a time when the UK's defence spending is under scrutiny, with concerns about the government's ability to meet its NATO commitment to spend 2% of GDP on defence.

The four remaining prisoners in the Guantanamo prison camp are to be released in the next few weeks, according to American officials. This is a continuation of Vice President Joe Biden's program to close the controversial detention camp. Guantanamo Bay, which has been in Cuba, has become the symbol of the United States's post-Sept. 11 war on terror. The camp was opened in 2002 and has been subject to criticism for the use of extraordinary renditions and the alleged mistreatment of prisoners. Over the years, many prisoners have been held without charge or trial, causing international condemnation and calls for its closure. In recent years, efforts have been made to reduce the population of the camp. Former President Barack Obama had promised to close the camp but faced resistance from Congress and could only carry out a partial withdrawal. Vice President Joe Biden has vowed to resume the process and the imminent release of four prisoners is a first step in fulfilling this promise. The identities of the four prisoners who are to be released have not been disclosed. American officials have stated that they are non-Yemeni nationals who have been cleared for transfer. They will be subject to monitoring and security restrictions in order to avoid the risks associated with a potential return to terrorism. The imminent release of the prisoners has been welcomed by human rights groups, but others have said that the camp should have been closed long ago and that more should have been done to remedy the human rights abuses that occurred in Guantanamo. There have also been concerns about the return to terrorism of former detainees, as some who were released from Guantanamo have subsequently rejoined terrorist groups. The release of the four prisoners is part of the current review of the remaining prisoners and the problems associated with transferring or judging them. The Biden administration has placed emphasis on the humane treatment of prisoners and compliance with international law and human rights standards. While the camp is closed, the fate of the remaining detainees and of the camp itself is unclear. The closure of Guantanamo would mark a significant change in American policy towards terrorism and close a chapter of the country's history that has been marked by controversy.

A renowned American composer has successfully recreated previously lost musical score by Johann Sebastian Bach, considered one of the greatest composers in history. The rediscovered work, titled "Gloria in excelsis Deo," is believed to have been composed by Bach during his time as Kapellmeister at court of Duke Wilhelm Ernst of Saxe-Weimar in early 18th century.

The reconstruction was accomplished by musicologist and composer Dr. Ruth Steiner, who spent years studying Bach's original manuscripts and researching historical records to piece together the missing parts of score. According to Dr. Steiner, process was like solving a complex puzzle, requiring meticulous attention to detail and deep understanding of Bach's composition style.

"It was an incredible challenge, but also a thrilling opportunity to bring this beautiful music back to life," said Dr. Steiner in an interview with the BBC. "Bach's music has been a source of inspiration for me throughout my career, and I felt a great responsibility to do justice to his vision."

The newly reconstructed "Gloria in excelsis Deo" is a large-scale choral work featuring multiple vocal soloists, choir, and orchestra. It showcases Bach's mastery of counterpoint and his ability to create intricate, interweaving melodies that blend together in rich tapestry of sound.

Dr. Steiner's reconstruction was made possible through her extensive analysis of surviving fragments from the original score, which had been thought to be lost forever. By carefully examining Bach's other works from same period, she was able to identify characteristic patterns and techniques that allowed her to fill in gaps and complete missing sections.

The completed score will receive its world premiere performance next month at Carnegie Hall in New York City, performed by Orchestra of St. Luke's and conducted by Maestro John Eliot Gardiner. The concert promises to be a once-in-a-lifetime experience for fans of classical music and a testament to enduring power of Bach's artistry.

The world's biggest consumer technology fair has opened in Las Vegas, with Microsoft's Bill Gates among those attending.

The Consumer Electronics Show (CES) is expected to attract 150,000 visitors during its four-day run.

Mr Gates will deliver a keynote speech on Wednesday, in which he is expected to unveil new products.

The CES is seen as barometer of health of the tech industry.

This year's show is being closely watched for signs of how sector is weathering global economic downturn.

"CES is always important show for Microsoft," said Steve Ballmer, company's chief executive, who is also attending the event.

"It's great opportunity for us to share our vision for how technology will improve people's lives and to show the progress we're making against that vision."

High-definition television (HDTV) is expected to be one of hottest topics at the show.

More than ever before, CES is about convergence - the coming together of different technologies," said Gary Shapiro, president and chief executive of the Consumer Electronics Association, which organises the event.

"This is year that high-definition television, the internet and the PC really start to come together."

Other products expected to be on display include ultra-thin laptops, netbooks - small, low-cost laptops - and e-readers, which allow users to download books and other publications electronically.

Giving financial gifts to children can be joyful experience, but it's important to consider potential impact on their development and well-being. While it may seem like easy way to show love and affection, excessive giving or inappropriate gifts can have negative consequences.

Research has shown that too much money given to young children can lead to a sense of entitlement and a lack of appreciation for the value of hard work. It can also create unrealistic expectations about future wealth and spending habits. Instead of focusing solely on material possessions, it's more beneficial to give experiences and opportunities that promote personal growth and learning.

In addition, certain types of gifts can be harmful if they are not age-appropriate or safe. For example, toys with small parts or sharp edges can pose choking hazards, while electronic devices can limit physical activity and social interaction. Parents should always carefully choose gifts that align with their child's interests and needs.

It's also worth considering the long-term effects of financial gifts on child's relationship with their parents. If parents rely heavily on gifts as a means of showing love and support, this can create pressure to continue giving at increasingly high levels, potentially leading to feelings of resentment or disappointment when these expectations cannot be met.

Instead of relying solely on financial gifts, parents can show their love and support through quality time, meaningful conversations, and acts of kindness. By prioritizing relationships over material possessions, we can help our children develop healthy attitudes towards money and build strong foundations for their future success.

Muslims across America are discussing their concerns about getting involved in the election process as the nation's First Muslim presidential candidate, Abdulrahman Muhammad, makes history with his candidacy. At the same time, Muslims are also talking about how they can contribute to the national conversation on religion and politics. A number of Muslim organizations have been working to encourage Muslim Americans to register and vote. These organizations include the Muslim Voter Project, the American Muslim Taskforce, and the Council on American-Islamic Relations.

in the 2020 election, Muslim voter Turnout increased by 13% from 2016. Muslims account for roughly 1.1% of the US population, or 3.45 million people, according to pew Research Center estimates. That figure is projected to reach Roughly 4 million by 2040. Muslim Americans Hail from a diverse range of backgrounds, with white Muslims accounting for 41% of the population, Black Muslims at 22%, and Asian Muslims at 20%.

Muslims Face discrimination when It comes to voting, according to a new study released by the Pew Research Center. The Study found that one-in-ten Muslim Americans say they have experienced discrimination when going to vote or participating in political campaigns. In addition, more than half of muslim Americans say they have Been subjected to religious discrimination in the Last year.

"With the Muslim candidate, We're allowing people to have a conversation about what Muslim-ness means in the United States," said Wajahat Ali, a comic and writer who published "The Muslim Bill of Rights" in 2017.

Muslim Americans are also increasingly concerned about the rise in hate crimes against their community. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, hate crimes against Muslims in the US increased by 50% in 2021.

"It's really important for Muslim Americans to vote because we have consistently Been the target of hate crimes and discrimination," said Dr. Zainab Chaudry, the Maryland director of the council on American-Islamic Relations.

But despite repeated warnings by the FBI, Israel will not give any details about what is under investigation and has refused comment on the arrests yet, according to a spokesman.

The number of smartphone security threats has doubled since last year and this looks unlikely to change soon, experts tell BBC's Newsbeat programme for younger audiences.

In the past three months there were several reports about hackers targeting more than one billion Android users via Google Play Store apps that infected thousands with so-called ransomware. Another problem has seen scammers creating fake versions of legitimate mobile networks’ apps which tricked people into handing over sensitive information or personal details. So what makes them vulnerable? “We are getting a lot closer… we just need someone who can put [the dots] together,” Professor Alan Woodward at Surrey University told Newsbeat. He specialises in cybersecurity and said he expected attacks on phones to escalate as they got smarter and their owner carried out increasingly sensitive transactions using their devices. In addition to these types of scams another serious threat comes from spyware developed by governments, says Prof Dan Wallach at Rice University in Houston, Texas.
More people switching to mobiles
Professor Alan Woodard, Centre for Cyber Security, Surrey University For example, firm FinFisher sells its Remote Control System (RCS) software to law enforcement agencies, but many researchers have warned it could be misused for espionage activities conducted against activists, dissidents or others deemed threatening by political regimes. In an interview with the BBC, Conservative Party Chairman Oliver Dowden stated that the party believes in giving people a second chance, and suggested that Archer could potentially be welcomed back into the party if he demonstrated genuine remorse for his past actions.

Archer, once a prominent Conservative MP and successful author, was forced to resign from Parliament in 1999 following his conviction. His political career had been marred by scandal, including allegations of financial impropriety and extramarital affairs. However, the charismatic Archer remains a divisive figure, with some arguing that his talents and popularity should not be overlooked.

Dowden's comments come amidst ongoing discussions within the Conservative Party about its future direction, following the UK's departure from the European Union and the COVID-19 pandemic. The party is grappling with issues such as internal divisions and the need to build a more inclusive image. Some party members believe that Archer's re-entry into the fold could help to rebuild the party's reputation and improve its standing with the public.

Critics, however, argue that embracing a figure like Archer would send a damageing message about the party's values and integrity. They argue that it is important for political parties to hold their members to high moral standards and to distance themselves from individuals with a history of criminal behaviour.

Archer's case raises important questions about rehabilitation and second chances in politics. While many believe in the principle of redemption, others argue that politicians should be held to a higher standard and that their past actions should have long-lasting consequences.

Ultimately, the decision on whether to welcome Archer back into the Conservative Party rests with its leaders and members. It remains to be seen whether they will take the door left open by Dowden or whether they will choose to move forward without the controversial figure.

Georgia's government has said it will pardon people concealing assets from the tax authorities, in bid to boost revenues.

The amnesty will run from 1 January to 31 March, and will cover undeclared bank accounts, property and other assets.

The government says it wants to bring "substantial amounts of money" back into economy.

Opposition parties have criticised the move, saying it will only benefit the rich.

Under scheme, people who come forward and declare their assets will not face prosecution.

Those who do not take advantage of the amnesty will face much tougher penalties if they are caught, government says.

The move comes as country's economy stagnates and the government struggles to meet its revenue targets.

Georgia's Finance Minister Nodar Khaduri said amnesty would raise about $200m (£120m).

"The purpose of this initiative is to ensure that all entrepreneurs and individuals who have been concealing their assets from the revenue service for different reasons come clean," he said.

"The state will benefit from this, as it will allow us to collect taxes which have not been paid."

Mr Khaduri said the money would be used to fund social welfare programmes.

The amnesty will not apply to any assets which have been acquired through criminal activities.

In the latest sign that Ukraine is shedding its Soviet past, Kyiv is to sell prized state-owned assets, including ports, airports, and coal and steel businesses whose production is key to the nation's economy. The sale is being overseen by government's Ministry of Economy and includes businesses in ports, such as Odesa and Mykolayiv, airports in Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipro, and country's largest steel and coal companies - Kryvyi Rih Iron Ore Enrichment Plant and SevGOK respectively. "The sale of state-owned enterprises has started," Economy Minister Yulia Svyrydenko said in statement on her Facebook page. "This is largest sale in the history of independent Ukraine." She added that more information on sale, whose value was not revealed, would be released soon. The assets will be sold using a "Dutch auction" method, where bidders compete to buy the property for the lowest price. Those who offer highest price win, but seller can decide to accept any or all bids. 

The ministry did not reveal who potential buyers were. The assets themselves are prized: Ukraine's ports are responsible for roughly 80 per cent of country's sea trade. The nation's coal industry, still a major contributor to the power grid, employs over 80,000 people. The steel industry, centred on Kryvyi Rih in south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region, employs 185,000 people directly and another 650,000 people indirectly. The sale comes amid a broader reorganisation of Ukraine's economy. Last month, Kyiv restarted sale of its stranded gas assets - gas storage facilities that were designed to work in tandem with now-defunct Soviet-era pipelines to Russia - which have been idle since Russia launched its invasion. Ukraine is also preparing to issue its first-ever state debt auction as it looks to refinance some of its sovereign debt. 

Kyiv has garnered over $5bn from Western donors since the Russian invasion, money that has gone towards supporting country's finances as it faces huge economic challenges. The finance ministry expects Ukraine's economy to shrink by about third this year, with the World Bank forecasting that the number of people living in poverty could more than double, to over 50 per cent of the population.

Britain's Foreign  Secretary Jack Straw has called for international agreement on stem cell research.

Mr Straw made  the appeal during a speech in  London on Monday, in  which he also announced £10m of UK government funding  for the work.

He said   ethical  concerns  must be addressed, but  stem cell research  could lead to treatments  for a range of diseases.

Mr Straw's remarks come amid a debate in the US over President Bush's  decision to restrict federal  funding  for the work.

'Hopeful advance'

The UK government has  said it will provide  £10m over  the  next three years for stem cell research using  human embryos.

Mr Straw  said ethical concerns  must   be considered

The move was criticised by  some  Christian groups, but was welcomed  by scientists.

During his speech, Mr Straw  said there was a "powerful argument" in favour of the work.

"The potential therapeutic benefits of stem cell research are  immensely exciting," he said.

"Our job now is to promote an internationally agreed  regulatory framework that will allow this research  to  proceed in  an ethical way."

He said the  UK government would be working with the US and European Union to try to reach  an agreement.

Mr Straw said the UK already had "robust" laws governing stem cell research, but  an international consensus was needed  to prevent a "race to the bottom" in ethical standards.

"No   government  should be deterred from taking  the right course  by the  fact that other countries have lower  ethical standards," he said.

'Diseases  cured'

Mr Straw  said the UK government  wanted to see the therapeutic  potential of stem cells realised, but insisted this must be done  in an ethical way.

"We  are not trying to second-guess  the public on this - we need a full and informed public  debate," he  said.

"And   we must not underestimate either  the difficulties  we face in reconciling the ethical  considerations, or the ground we have to make up."

Mr Straw said he hoped stem cell research would lead  to  treatments for diseases  such  as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's, as well as spinal injuries.

"I am  in no doubt that this is a hopeful  advance, with the potential to  bring immeasurable benefits  to some of the most  vulnerable people  in our society," he  said.

Microsoft has recently caught the blogging bug and is expanding its offerings in the blogging world. The tech giant has announced the acquisition of Nuance Communications, a company specialising in speech recognition and artificial intelligence technology. This move will help Microsoft further integrate these capabilities into its existing products and services, including its popular voice assistant, Cortana.

The acquisition of Nuance Communications is seen as a strategic move by Microsoft to strengthen its presence in the healthcare industry. Nuance is a leading provider of speech and imageing solutions for the healthcare sector, and Microsoft aims to leverage this expertise to improve healthcare experiences for both providers and patients. The acquisition will also give Microsoft access to Nuance's extensive customer base, which includes iconic healthcare organisations and top retailers.

Blogging has become increasingly important in the digital landscape, with individuals and businesses alike using blogs to share their perspectives, promote products and services, and connect with their audiences. Microsoft recognises the potential of blogging and is keen to enhance its offerings in this area. The company has long been a player in the blogging space through its ownership of blogging platform LinkedIn, but with the acquisition of Nuance, Microsoft intends to further strengthen its capabilities and expand its reach.

The growing demand for voice-based interactions and the integration of artificial intelligence technologies have made speech recognition a key focus for many tech companies, including Microsoft. With the addition of Nuance's technology, Microsoft can improve its voice recognition capabilities, making Cortana and other voice-controlled services more efficient and accurate. This integration can greatly benefit users by providing them with more seamless and natural interactions with digital devices and services.

As part of the acquisition, Microsoft plans to integrate Nuance's technologies into various Microsoft products, including Azure, Teams, and Dynamics 365. This move will allow Microsoft to provide enhanced AI-driven solutions across multiple industries, including healthcare, finance, and customer service.

With this bold move, Microsoft is positioning itself as a dominant player in the blogging and speech recognition space. By acquiring Nuance Communications, the tech giant is not only expanding its offerings but also gaining a significant competitive advantage over its rivals. It will be interesting to see how Microsoft leverages this acquisition to further revolutionise the way we interact with technology and how it impacts the blogging and communication landscape as a whole.

Sir Steven Redgrave, Britain's most successful Olympian, has announced his plans to compete in at least two major rowing events this year, marking his return to competitive racing after a brief retyrement.

Redgrave, who won five consecutive gold medals at five Olympic Games between 1984 and 2000, retyred from professional rowing after winning his fifth gold medal in Sydney. But now he is set to make a comeback, eyeing the World Cup regattas in Munich and Lucerne, Switzerland. He will also participate in the British Rowing Championships in July as part of the British team.

The 43-year old athlete confessed that it was difficult for him to stay away from the sport for long and expressed excitement about rejoining his crew mates. "I have missed being part of a team," said Redgrave, adding that he was looking forward to racing again. His coxless four team, which includes Matt Pinsent, Tim Foster, and James Cracknell, will be hoping to continue their winning streak, having been unbeaten since coming together before the Athens Olympics in 2004. They are expected to face stiff competition, but if they succeed, it could pave the way for an eighth world championship title later this year. Redgrave admits there may be other international events lined up, but nothing is confirmed yet. However, his participation in the World Cup circuit would increase speculation that he might try for another Olympic gold medal in Beijing in 2008. The veteran rower, considered one of Great Britain’s greatest-ever athletes, declines to comment on such prospects though.

BBC News has removed video footage of  an activist interrupting   the mayor of Bristol's speech at a memorial.

Campaigner Sabina McFadden claims  she was wrongly arrested after she stepped onto a stage and  held  up  a banner at  the We Are Bristol rally.

The BBC obtained  permission from Ms. McFadden to use the footage.

However, it has since  been asked to take it down by   one of the  people  who appeared  in it.

They have told the BBC they were not aware they  were being filmed at the time.

The footage showed Ms. McFadden interrupting Bristol Mayor Marvin Rees as he spoke at the  memorial to those who have died with coronavirus.

She was arrested on suspicion  of causing a public nuisance but was not charged with any crime.

She  told  the BBC she was pursuing legal action against Avon and Somerset Police and said she "would have expected better" from the corporation.

"I  don't believe the BBC should be working with the police to suppress freedom of expression  and interfere with open justice,"  she said.

The BBC  is editing the video clip, which is on the  BBC News  website and has been used   on   television, to remove the individual who has  raised  the issue.

A BBC  spokesman  said: "We have  always stated that  we would only show the footage  of Ms. McFadden if we obtained permission from all those appearing   in  it.

"In this   case, we  have  been asked by one individual - who did not know they were on camera - to  take down the footage. We are happy  to  do so."

Ms. McFadden  said she was  "delighted" the BBC had  "done  the   right thing".

She said the interference   with   her protest - which she staged to draw attention  to the deaths  of Afro-Caribbean people in  the city from coronavirus - was "an infringement of my human rights".

The BBC has also removed a social media post promoting the  video.

Hundreds of thousands of Beijingers who own private cars - a relatively rare possession in China - have complained that the cost of parking fees is soaring.
The capital city - which is home to more than 18 million people - is a notoriously congested place and is struggling to come up with ways to ease traffic bottlenecks.
There has been a spate of car accidents in Beijing in recent months amid complaints that the city's one-way traffic system does not help.
"It's impossible that parking fees will be doubled overnight," said one of the commenters.
"It's not the government's money that the people pay taxes for, so it is a complete absurdity to say that the city government still needs to cut costs on our behalf."
A number of parking businesses have been forced to go out of business recently.
The city's administration says it is increasing the enforcement of parking rules and the enforcement of fines, which it said was "for the good of people".
It said it was focusing on the most serious problems that pose a danger to public safety.

The British textiles industry could lose tens of thousands of jobs in the next few years, an industry body has said.

The Textile Institute said faster automation and the war in Ukraine were significant factors in the expected job losses.

The institute said advances in artificial intelligence (AI) would especially hurt smaller companies.

It called for government support to help the sector adapt.

The institute's CEO, Laxton Lam, said: "Numerous factors, including accelerating automation, the war in Ukraine, and the rise of AI and digitalisation, have compounded this challenge."

"Smaller companies are less able to invest in new technologies and processes and face going out of business," he added.

The institute said there was a "real risk" that the textile industry's 8,000 jobs could halve by 2027.

It added that the sector, which had already been struggling with labour shortages and rising costs before the pandemic, had been hit harder than others by rising energy bills.

IBM has announced that it will release over 5,000 software patents to the public domain in an effort to encourage collabouration and innovation in technology. The company said that these patents are no longer needed by them as they focus on new technologies and business models.

The move is part of IBM's commitment to contribute to the open-source community and foster creativity in tech research. It is worth noting that some of these patents could have significant impacts in areas such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain technology, and cloud computing.

"By making our intellectual property publicly available at no cost, we hope to accelerate R&D and help drive innovations that benefit society," said Arvind Krishna, Senior Vice President for Research at IBM. "We believe this step represents a fundamental shift towards a more collabourative approach to innovation."

Over 40% of IBM's total patent portfolio, or over 17,500 patents, were made public in May last year. This move sparked significant interest among researchers and companies looking to commercialise new technologies through collabouration with IBM.

According to John Enochson, CEO of OpenLogic, an industry leader in open source licencing solutions: "One of the greatest challenges in building large scale systems and applications is navigating complex intellectual property landscapes. With these patents being released to the public domain, developers can draw upon this rich trove of knowledge without risk of infringement."

With the growing importance of AI, blockchain, and other emerging technologies in today's digital landscape, this announcement from IBM is sure to be met with enthusiasm by the global tech community.

Britain's world number one Billy Monger will not be defending his Paralympic title in Tokyo after challenging year saw him miss out on qualifying.

The 19-year-old, who was born with no legs, won the 100m and 200m T53 wheelchair racing events at Rio 2016.

But he has struggled with his eyesight since surgery after last year's World Championships and has now "turned his focus" to 2018's Commonwealth Games in Australia.

"It's been a bit of rollercoaster," said Monger, who set new world record in the 800m at 2016 Paralympics.

"I've really struggled with my eyesight since surgery - I've been trying to focus on track and not the medical side of things."

The double Paralympic champion has undergone eight surgeries in 12 months to correct his eyesight but now faces a wait to see if he will require further treatment.

"It's been tough decision to make but these things happen and you've got to roll with punches," added Monger, who also won bronze in the 4x100m relay in Rio.

"I'm 20 years old, I've got rest of my life to try and achieve what I want to achieve.

"I'm not going to sacrifice my long-term health. It's not worth it for sprint race."

Monger spent much of 2017 undergoing rehabilitation for the surgeries he had undergone, which meant he missed bulk of the wheelchair racing season.

And he has now accepted that he will not be able to race at Tokyo 2020 Paralympics.

"It's not going to happen, I'm not going to be able to race at the level I need to," he said.

"I've missed too much of the season, I wouldn't be able to get myself in the shape I need to be in.

"It's heartbreaking, but these things happen and I'm looking forward to racing in 2021."

While he will not be racing in Tokyo, Monger said he is hopeful of being able to compete at the Paralympic Games in 2024 in Paris.

"It gives me three years to get my body in the shape it needs to be in and I'm really excited about that," he said.

"It's going to be nice, comfortable pace. I'll be able to ease myself into it and I'm excited to see what I can achieve."

LONDON - The government has announced that the EU membership referendum will be held on Thursday, June 23rd with voters asked to decide wether or not Britain should leave the European Union.

The Electoral Commission said it was satisfied with the wording of the ballot paper which reads: 'Should the United Kingdom remain a member of the European Union?'

David Cameron who is campaigning for Britons to vote in favor of staying within Europe hailed this as an historic moment and urged people across UK to take part in what he called one of most important decisions facing country since World War II.

However opposition leader Jeremy Corbyn warned against leaving saying exit would cause economic uncertainty and damage British economy while Scottish National Party's Nicola Sturgeon argued Scotland must have right choose its own future outside England-dominated union.

With just over three months untill polling day campaigners from both sides are gearing up their efforts ahead of what many predict could be closest fought election in recent history.

Drinks group Diageo is to buy US wine company Beam Inc in a deal worth £13.4bn ($17.81bn).

The maker of Johnnie Walker whisky is paying £4.55bn ($6.4bn) in cash and shares for the maker of Jim Beam bourbon and Courvoisier cognac.

 Shares in London-based Diageo closed up 1.5% on the news.

Diageo said the deal would transform it into the world's leading spirits company by "incremental sales".

The company said it would accelerate its expansion in key growth markets such as the US and China.

Diageo has been advised by Goldman Sachs, while JPMorgan and PJT Park Hill have worked with Beam on the deal.

The deal comes as the drinks industry faces slowing growth in Europe and increasing pressure from governments seeking to counter binge drinking.

Last year, Diageo held talks with Guinness maker Heineken over a possible merger of their drinks businesses. However, those discussions broke down over price and because of the complexity of merging the two firms.

At the end of 2013, Diageo had sales of £6.7bn and operating profits of £2.7bn. It employs about 30,000 people.

Beam, which is listed on the New York Stock Exchange, reported sales of about $4.3bn and operating profits of about $660m in the year to 31 March. It employs about 5,000 people.

David Beckham has ruled out pursuing a career in football management, despite widespread speculation that he could follow in the footsteps of his former coach at Manchester United, Alex Ferguson. The retired England captain and his wife Victoria have been linked with a number of clubs both in Britain and abroad, but speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Beckham made it clear that managing was not something he wanted to do. "I'm enjoying my role as an ambassador for the game," he said, adding that coaching or managing would be too much pressure. "It's about winning week in, week out," he explained. "There are so many pressures involved." Instead, Mr. Beckham revealed that he hopes to continue working closely with charities around the world using his profile to bring attention to important causes. When asked if there were any areas where he felt particularly passionate about making a difference, David smiled wistfully: "Children always hold a special place in my heart" - words guaranteed to make every parent watching feel proud of their own offspring.

A new technology utilizing lasers is being implemented to bridge network gaps in areas where traditional internet connectivity is unreliable or non-existent. This innovative solution uses lasers to transmit data through light, allowing for high-speed internet access in even the most remote or underdeveloped areas.

The technology, known as free-space optical communication (FSO), uses lasers to transmit data through light over short distances. This is accomplished by directing a laser beam between two points, creating a network link that can support speeds of up to 100 Gbps. The lasers are equipped with advanced sensors and motion-tracking systems to ensure accurate and reliable data transmission, even in adverse wether conditions.

The use of lasers to bridge network gaps has already shown promising results in several pilot projects around the world. In Africa, for example, a team of researchers from the University of Cambridge and the University of KwaZulu-Natal successfully established a high-speed internet connection between two towns using FSO technology. The connection, which spanned a distance of 2.5 kilometers, was able to support speeds of up to 10 Gbps.

In addition to its potential in rural areas, FSO technology also has applications in urban settings. In densely populated cities, laser-based networks can be used to create a mesh of interconnected nodes, providing a more reliable and efficient internet connection. This can be particularly useful in areas where traditional network infrastructure is overburdened or unreliable.

Russian athlete Tatyana Isinbayeva has set a new world record in the women's pole vault at the World Athletics Championships in Doha, Qatar.

Isinbayeva cleared a height of 2.14 meters (16 feet 1.75 inches) on her second attempt, breaking the previous world record of 9.01 meters set by her teammate Yelena Sokolova at the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

The 32-year-old Isinbayeva, who has won four Olympic gold medals in the pole vault, was visibly emotional after the jump, hugging her coach and teammates before taking a bow to the cheering crowd.

"I am so happy, I can't believe it," Isinbayeva said after the competition. "I have been working so hard for this moment, and it has finally come."

Isinbayeva's performance was widely praised by fellow athletes and commentators, with many hailing it as one of the greatest moments in the history of the sport.

"Tatyana Isinbayeva is a true legend," said American pole vaulter Sandi Morris, who finished second in the competition. "She has always been an inspiration to me and to so many other athletes around the world."

Isinbayeva's victory in the pole vault was one of several stunning performances by Russian athletes at the World Athletics Championships, which have been held in Doha since October 3th.

The most immediate problem is that there's no way to develop games for the new consoles without spending a fortune on hardware. The current generation of consoles uses off-the-shelf components, but the new consoles are using custom-made hardware that's exclusive to each console.

That means that developers will need to buy both a PS4 and an Xbox One just to be able to develop for both consoles. And that's assuming they can even find a way to get their hands on the hardware in the first place.

The other problem is that the new consoles are going to be very difficult to develop for. The extra RAM is going to be a challenge to work with, and the new consoles are also introducing new features like support for 4K resolution and multi-threaded processors.

All of this is going to result in some very expensive development costs, and it's going to make it even harder for smaller developers to compete.

So, if you're looking forward to the next generation of consoles, be prepared for some big problems.

In an unexpected move, winemaker Jacob's Creek has rejected a takeover bid from global brewery giant Foster's Group. 

The merger would have created one of the largest wine companies in the world, with an estimated value of over $4 billion. However, sources close to Jacob's Creek say that the company's management team and board of directors decided against the proposal after careful consideration. Foster's had been offering to purchase the remaining 50% stake it doesn't already own for AUD$1.35 billion ($966 million), but according to reports, shareholders were concerned about potential cost cuts and job losses as well as cultural differences between the two brands. 

In a statement released yesterday, President and CEO of Fosters, Trevor O'Hoy said: “We continue to believe that merging our businesses makes sense,” he added however also saying ”should we fail” which shows their disapointment on this turn off event. 

Nevertheless, analysts predict that foster’s might look at other opportunities to grow its beverages business including beer, cider or even spirits. For now though, Adelaide-based Jacob's Creek remains independent and focused on continuing to produce high quality wines underits famous brand name."

The United States trade deficit reached a record high in 2004, according to the latest data released by Commerce Department. The gap between what the US imports and what it exports rose to $617.7 billion, 24% increase from the previous year. This marks fourth consecutive year of widening trade deficits for the world's largest economy.

The surge in trade deficit was primarily driven by a surge in imports, which rose by 18% to $1.5 trillion. The increase in imports was largely due to strong consumer demand for foreign goods, particularly in the areas of electronics, clothing, and automobiles. At the same time, US exports only grew by 12% to $891.3 billion, failing to keep pace with the growth in imports.

The widening trade deficit has raised concerns among economists and policymakers, who fear that it could have negative implications for US economy in the long run. Critics argue that trade deficit reflects a lack of competitiveness in American industries and reliance on foreign goods. They also worry that large trade deficit could put downward pressure on the value of the US dollar and lead to inflation.

The record trade deficit has also fueled debates about the impact of globalization on US economy. Supporters of globalization argue that the trade deficit is natural consequence of globalized economy and that it brings benefits such as access to cheaper goods and increased consumer choice. However, critics argue that the trade deficit is sign of unfair trade practices by other countries, such as currency manipulation and intellectual property theft.

The US government has taken steps to address the trade deficit, including negotiating trade agreements and imposing tariffs on certain imports. However, these measures have been met with mixed results and have not been able to significantly reduce the trade gap.

Looking ahead, economists are divided on outlook for US trade deficit. Some believe that the deficit will continue to widen as long as consumer demand for foreign goods remains strong. Others are more optimistic, pointing to the potential for increased exports as global economy recovers from impact of COVID-19 pandemic.

Overall, the record trade deficit in 2004 highlights challenges faced by US in maintaining balanced trade relationship with the rest of world. It also underscores need for policymakers to address the underlying factors contributing to deficit and to promote policies that support domestic industries and exports.

With this unique feature, developers have been able to create games that encourage players to interact with the touch screen, bringing a new level of engagement and immersion. This has led to a wide variety of game genres being available, from puzzle games to RPGs, ensuring there is something for everyone.

Its sleek design and compact size make it portable and easy to carry around, allowing gamers to indulge in their favorite titles wherever they go. Furthermore, the console supports wireless connectivity, enabling players to connect with friends and compete against each other in multiplayer games.

These games, combined with the unique features of the console, have created a buzz among gamers and are expected to drive sales even further.

Industry analysts believe the Nintendo DS has the potential to revolutionize the handheld gaming market in Europe. With its innovative features, wide range of game genres, and strong lineup of titles, the console is poised to capture the attention and loyalty of gamers across the continent. Its competitive pricing compared to other handheld gaming devices is also a factor that is attracting both casual and hardcore gamers alike.

As the Nintendo DS makes its Euro debut, it is expected to create a gaming revolution, providing countless hours of entertainment and fun for gamers of all ages. With its unique features, impressive graphics, and an extensive library of games, the future looks bright for Nintendo's latest handheld gaming console in Europe. Gamers can now rejoice as they finally get their hands on this highly anticipated device and experience the next level of portable gaming.
