Former Manchester United manager Jose Mourinho will not face a Football Association charge over alleged racist behaviour towards winger Antonio Valencia. 

The FA concluded its investigation into the incident on Wednesday, which occurred in November 2018. It is understood the evidence package presented to the governing body's independent commission concluded Mourinho's actions did not constitute racist behaviour. United have confirmed that their review of the incident - which saw Mourinho publicly shame Valencia over his poor physical condition - has also now concluded. 

A club spokesman said: "Manchester United has thoroughly reviewed the incident involving Jose Mourinho and Antonio Valencia on 20 November 2018. 

"The club concluded its investigation into the incident in January 2019 and shared its findings with the FA. "Manchester United does not condone discriminatory behaviour in any form and provides equal employment opportunities, irrespective of race, gender, religion, and ability." The incident involving Mourinho and Valencia occurred at United's training ground at Carrington. A documentary filmed by the club for their MUTV channel showed Mourinho shouting at Valencia - who had just returned from international duty with Ecuador - and telling him he was not going to be selected to play in a game against Liverpool. 

The manager told the player he was "not a left-back or a right-back" and that "he has to change his career" before sarcastically adding "good player, good man". Valencia, who made 432 appearances for United between 2009 and 2019, was reduced to tears by the confrontation. 

In October, a similarly explosive exchange between Mourinho and another United player, Luke Shaw, formed part of the evidence used by the FA in their successful charge against him for using foul and abusive language. 

The left-back was sacked as manager of Tottenham earlier in the season, with the club citing "very disappointing" results as the reason for his dismissal.

The UK's brewing industry is facing a significant downturn, With profits going flat as the sector grapples with the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic and changing consumer habits.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), the industry has seen a sharp decline In sales, with many breweries struggling to stay Afloat. The BBPA estimates that beer sales in pubs fell by 56% in 2020, equivalent to a loss of £7.8bn.

The closure of pubs and restaurants During the lockdowns has hit the industry hard, with many breweries having to pour away unsold beer. Even with the easing of restrictions, the industry is still facing challenges. Social distancing measures mean pubs can serve fewer customers, and many people are still wary of going out.

"the pandemic has been devastating for our industry. We've seen breweries of all sizes suffering, from the smallest craft brewers to the largest national producers," said Emma McClarkin, Chief Executive of the BBPA.

Changing consumer habits are also affecting the industry. There has been a shift towards low and no-alcohol beers, with sales of these products increasing by 30% in The last year, according to market research firm Nielsen. This trend is expected To continue, Putting further pressure on traditional brewers.

The industry is also grappling with rising costs. The price of barley, a key ingredient in beer, has increased due to poor harvests and increased demand from China. in addition, the end of the Brexit transition period has led to increased costs and complexity for brewers exporting to the EU.

Despite these challenges, some breweries are finding ways to adapt. Many have pivoted to Online sales and home Deliveries, while others Are experimenting with new products To cater To changing consumer tastes.

However, the BBPA warns That without further Support From the government, many breweries could go out of business. The association is calling for A cut in beer duty and an extension of Business rates relief to help the industry recover.

"The brewing industry is a vital Part of the UK economy, supporting thousands of jobs and contributing billions to the treasury each year. It's crucial that the government does all it can to support our brewers and pubs in these challenging times," said McClarkin.

The brewing industry's woes are a stark reminder of the wider impact of the pandemic on the UK economy. As the country begins to emerge from lockdown, the challenge will be to ensure that industries like brewing can regain their fizz.

The  US government is  reportedly planning to increase fines for television broadcasters who violate indecency regulations.  The move comes amid growing concerns about the content being shown on mainstream television, particularly during hours when children are likely  to  be watching.

The Federal Communications Commission  (FCC),  the body responsible for  regulating interstate and international communications by radio, television, wire, satellite, and cable,  is said to be behind the proposed  increase. The FCC has not yet confirmed the reports, but it is understood that the fines could be raised significantly.

Currently,  the maximum fine for a single violation  of indecency regulations is $325,000. However, this could  be  increased to as much as $500,000 if  the proposed  changes are  implemented.  The move is seen as a clear signal that the US government is   taking a tougher stance on the issue of television  indecency.

The FCC defines indecency as "language or material  that, in context, depicts or describes, in  terms patently offensive  as measured  by contemporary community standards for the broadcast  medium, sexual or excretory organs or activities." Broadcasters are prohibited from  airing  indecent content between 6 a.m.  and 10 p.m., when there is a reasonable  risk that children may   be in the  audience.

The  proposed increase  in fines has  been met with mixed reactions. Some argue that  it is a necessary step to protect   children from inappropriate  content, while others believe it is an infringement  on freedom of speech and artistic expression.

The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), a  trade  association that advocates on   behalf  of America's broadcasters, has yet to comment  on  the proposed changes. However,  the organization has previously argued that the current fines are  already a  significant deterrent and that further increases are  unnecessary.

The FCC's indecency rules have been the subject of controversy in  the past. Critics argue that  the rules are vague and subjective, making  it   difficult for broadcasters to  know  what content is considered indecent.  However, supporters  argue that the rules  are  necessary  to protect children  and uphold societal standards.

The proposed increase in fines is expected to  be discussed  at the next FCC meeting. If approved, the changes could   come into effect as early as  next year.

Gordon Brown has announced that he will present his annual budget on Wednesday, 16th March 2011. The Chancellor made the announcement in Parliament today as part of his autumn statement outlining government spending plans for the next two years.

The decision to set a specific date for this year's budget comes after months of speculation about when exactly it would be presented. Some had speculated that Mr Brown might delay the budget until after the local elections in May, but he appears to have opted instead for an earlier timetable.

In making the announcement, Mr Brown said that he wanted to give businesses and households as much notice as possible about any changes to taxation or public spending that may be contained within the budget. He also stressed the importance of maintaining fiscal discipline at a time when Britain is still grappling with high levels of debt and inflationary pressures.

While details of what specifically will be included in this year's budget remain under wraps, sources close to the chancellor suggest that there could be significant announcements related to tax cuts and infrastructure investment aimed at stimulating economic growth. However, given the current state of the nation's finances, it remains unclear how much leeway Mr Brown will have to implement such measures.

Overall, analysts are expecting this year's budget to be one of the most closely watched in recent memory, particularly given the ongoing debate over Britain's long-term economic strategy and the role that government policy should play in shaping it. With just three weeks to go before the big day, all eyes now turn to Westminster and the chancellor's office, eager to see what proposals Mr Brown has in store for Britain's taxpayers and economy alike.

India has banned 26 energy projects as part of a protest on corruption in the power industry.

The National Growth and Reform Council (NDRC) noted the projects were worth a combined $26bn (£16bn).

It comes after the nation's top prosecutor opened an inquiry into the world's two largest power companies.

The NDRC stated the projects had been suspended because of "alleged defects".

The projects included a $6.4bn coal-fired energy plant in the Outer Mongolian province and a $3.8bn hydropower station in the southern region of Mongolia.

The NDRC stated it will not investigate the role of representatives from the nation's electricity regulator, the National Nuclear Agency (NEA), in the projects.

The NEA has come under criticism in several years after it was reported that some of its leaders had offered bribes.

The crackdown on corruption in the energy industry is part of a wider campaign by the Indian state to root out graft.

Next year, the nation's top court opened an inquiry into the world's four largest energy companies - State Power, Guangdong Central Electric Grid and Shanghai Huaneng Company.

The companies have been accused of using their monopoly power to extort cash from customers and clients.

Boris Johnson has apologised for the gaolings of two British citizens in Hong Kong, as he faced criticism over the UK's handling of the situation in the territory.

The Prime Minister made the apology during a joint press conference with Chinese Premier Xi Jinping in Beijing, where he was on a two-day visit to strengthen ties between the two countries.

Johnson's apology came after the gaoling of two British nationals, Simon Cheng and Michael Vaughan, on charges of "pornography" and "obscene acts", respectively. The men, who were arrested in August, have denied any wrongdoing and say they were targeted because of their British citizenship.

"I want to make it absolutely clear that the UK government does not condone any form of criminal activity," Johnson said. By John Smith, writer, London

Imagine viewing television without a TV set.

In a motel hotel, you prop your phone on the bedside table, slide the desk stool over, and settle in to see the big match.

There's no need to log in to any streaming service. Then, you dial a cell number.

A familiar chime indicates the phone is disconnected and, finally, the match disappears on your cell's screen. You watch the game, Commercial breaks show hotel adverts. When the match finishes you hang up.

It looks far-fetched but in fact, it is still possible. In the UK, the telephone number belongs to the hotel. They are trialling the idea to deliver in-room entertainment to visitors.

And it's not just restaurants that are involved in this technology. In fact, it's not just TV. This is phone-casting - a manner of displaying video content on any phone, wherever you are, when you want.

How does it work?

The science behind phone-casting has not been around since the 1980s. But a lack of bandwidth and the low price of calls meant it eventually went off.

Meanwhile, UK-based company App Shui is betting that the time is now right to get the software back up to date.

The company has invented a way of streaming high-quality audio content over the mobile network, and it works with any phone, on any network.

"We are introducing something new and different to the industry that hasn't been done before," App Shui's Chief Manager, Mark Smith, informed the BBC.

Phone-casting: How it works

App Shui has devised a way to digitise audio material and break it up into small packets of data.

It then sends each packet individually over the mobile network. The procedure is halted at the other end, and the video is reconstructed on the phone screen.

"We use the phone number as a means to authenticate and connect two ends together," explains Dr Collins. "And then we use the telephone network to transmit the information."

The system now runs on a standard 03 phone number, and works on any mobile, if it is iOS, Android, or Linux.

Cybersecurity experts have warned that malicious web links are playing a significant role in the spread of computer viruses, putting both individuals and businesses at risk. These toxic web links, often hidden in seemingly harmless emails or text messages, can infect devices with malware, ransomware, or other types of harmful software. 

Once clicked, these links can give hackers access to sensitive information, including bank details and personal data. 

According to a recent report by cybersecurity firm, Cybereason, there has been a significant increase in the number of these malicious links over the past year. 

The report suggests that the shift to remote working due to the COVID-19 pandemic may have contributed to this rise, as hackers exploit vulnerabilities in home networks and less secure devices. "Working from home has blurred the lines between personal and professional use of technology," said Lior Div, CEO of Cybereason. 

"This has created new opportunities for cybercriminals to infiltrate networks and access sensitive data." 

The report also highlighted that these toxic links are becoming increasingly sophisticated, often mimicking legitimate websites or services to trick users into clicking on them. This technique, known as phishing, is a common method used by cybercriminals to steal personal information. In response to this growing threat, cybersecurity experts are urging individuals and businesses to take preventative measures. 

These include regularly updating software, using strong and unique passwords, and being cautious of any unexpected or suspicious emails or messages. "Education is key in preventing these attacks," said Div. "Users need to be aware of the risks and know how to spot potential threats. Businesses should also invest in robust cybersecurity measures and ensure their employees are adequately trained." 

The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has also issued guidance on how to stay safe online. It recommends using two-factor authentication where possible, regularly backing up data, and reporting any suspicious activity. 

As the digital landscape continues to evolve, the threat posed by toxic web links and other forms of cybercrime is likely to increase. It is therefore crucial that individuals and businesses remain vigilant and take the necessary steps to protect themselves online.

Singer Courtney Love has avoided jail time after pleading guilty to disorderly conduct charges stemming from a confrontation with a flight attendant on a plane last year.

Love, 56, was sentenced to 12 months of probation and ordered to pay a $500 fine by a court in Los Angeles. She had faced up to 180 days in jail for the misdemeanor charge.

According to court documents, Love was accused of verbally abusing a flight attendant and attempting to physically confront her on a flight from London to Los Angeles in August 2022. The oil markets have rallies strongly following weekend of intense fighting in Libya.

Brent crude rose $2.01 to $117.48 a barrel, while US crude was up $1.89 at $107.79.

The price had earlier risen by as much as $2.50, taking both contracts to their highest levels since 28 February.

Libyan output has all but stopped amid the unrest, removing around 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) from world markets.

"This is a continuation of yesterday's move on back of Libyan crisis," said Chris Whewell, an analyst at commodities research grouptradeview.

"It's very difficult to see how things could settle down quickly in Libya. We could see prices move higher in the short term."

The price of gold rose to new record high of $1,438.40 ounce on Monday.

The country is now only Opec member not to be exporting oil, according to International Energy Agency.

Cybersecurity experts have warned that toxic web links are playing a significant role in the spread of viruses and malware. These malicious links, often disguised as legitimate websites or emails, are being used by hackers to gain unauthorized access to personal and sensitive information.

The rise of remote working and increased reliance on digital platforms during the COVID-19 pandemic has created a fertile ground for cybercriminals to exploit. With more people working from home and conducting their daily activities online, the number of phishing attacks and malware infections has surged.

Phishing attacks, in particular, have become increasingly sophisticated, making it harder for individuals to distinguish between genuine and malicious links. Hackers are using social engineering techniques to trick users into clicking on these toxic links, which then lead to the installation of malware on their devices. Once infected, hackers can gain access to personal data, financial information, and even control the victim's device remotely.

The consequences of falling victim to these toxic web links can be severe. Not only can individuals suffer financial losses due to identity theft or fraudulent transactions, but businesses can also face significant damage to their reputation and financial stability. Moreover, the spread of viruses and malware can disrupt critical infrastructure, such as healthcare systems or government networks, leading to potential chaos and compromising public safety.

To combat this growing threat, cybersecurity experts are urging individuals and organizations to remain vigilant and adopt best practices for online safety. This includes being cautious when clicking on links, especially those received through emails or messages from unknown sources. Verifying the authenticity of websites before entering personal information or making online transactions is also crucial.

Furthermore, keeping software and antivirus programs up to date can help protect against known vulnerabilities and malware. Regularly backing up important data and files is another essential step in mitigating the impact of a potential cyberattack.

In addition to individual efforts, governments and tech companies are also taking action to tackle this issue. Increased investment in cybersecurity infrastructure, public awareness campaigns, and stricter regulations are being implemented to curb the spread of viruses and malware through toxic web links.

As the world becomes increasingly interconnected, the threat of cyberattacks and the role of toxic web links in spreading viruses cannot be underestimated. It is crucial for individuals, businesses, and governments to work together to strengthen cybersecurity measures and protect against this ever-evolving threat.

A construction behemoth has agreed to a multimillion-pound settlement to cover damages caused by exposure to asbestos, marking one of the largest payouts of its kind in history.

The company, whose identity has been withheld due to ongoing legal proceedings, had reportedly used asbestos, a dangerous and now widely banned building material, in several of its projects up to the 1980s.

Asbestos, if disturbed, can release harmful fibres which can lead to serious diseases like mesothelioma, a form of cancer that primarily affects the lining of the lungs. Thousands of former employees, contractors and clients claimed to have been exposed to the dangerous material.

After many years of denial and challenging court proceedings, the building giant has finally capitulated and agreed to a substantial settlement. While the exact figure has not been released, sources close to the case say it would be in the range of several million pounds, setting a new precedent in asbestos-related litigation.

"This is a momentous day for all those who have suffered due to the company’s negligence and historical use of asbestos," stated a lawyer for the plaintiffs. "Many of our clients have been waiting for this day for years, and hopefully, this settlement will give them some sense of justice."

It is estimated that asbestos has been a contributing factor in over 5000 deaths annually in the UK, with previous occupational exposure primarily in manufacturing and construction industries being a major risk factor.

This landmark case is expected to pave the way for future claims from those affected by similar negligence.

The UK started banning the use of asbestos from 1985 and fully prohibited its use, importation, or supply in 1999. However, many buildings constructed prior to these bans may still contain asbestos. Today, asbestos exposure often occurs during refurbishment or demolition works of these older buildings.

This settlement might send shock waves through the construction industry, potentially triggering similar lawsuits against companies that previously used asbestos. The construction giant will also need to review its prior practices and ensure that all future operations abide by health and safety regulations.

Health and safety campaigners lauded the settlement as a "significant victory", adding that it served as a stark reminder for businesses about the serious consequences of disregarding their obligations towards employee health and safety.

The unnamed building giant is reportedly considering appealing the settlement, although legal experts have suggested that such an attempt is unlikely to be successful.

A new postponement to the implementation of new EU privacy laws is not expected to effect organisations that have already begun preparing for them, experts say.
The introduction of the controversial Data Protection Directive has been delayed for a second time.

The European Union (EU) has announced that it will hold a referendum on its future relationship with the UK in 2019, following Brexit negotiations.

If the majority of voters choose to stay, then the UK's current membership status will continue as before. However, if the majority choose to leave, then the UK will have to negotiate new terms for its departure from the EU. This announcement comes after months of speculation about when the referendum would be held and what form it would take. 

Some had called for a two-stage process, whereby the UK first left the EU and then applied to rejoin under different rules. Others had argued that such a process could lead to confusion and uncertainty, and that a single referendum was needed to clarify the situation once and for all.

So, Halo 2 not only revolutionized gaming industry, but it also had significant impact on internet usage and paved the way for the online gaming boom that we see today.

A new virus has been discovered that can  infect  Windows machines and spread to other computers, according to security experts. The malware, called W32/Worm, was found in an online file sharing service and is being  used by cyber criminals to distribute ransomware.  It spreads through email  attachments or  via  malicious links on websites. The   virus is  designed to encrypt files on infected systems  and  then demands payment for their release. The ransom amount varies depending  on how much  data has been  encrypted. If  the  victim pays up, they will be able to access their files again but only after  paying another fee. The virus also makes it impossible to remove the infection without paying  the ransom.

This is not the first time  we have seen this   type of malware. Back in 2014,  researchers at Kaspersky Lab discovered a similar  piece of malware called WannaCry which  spread across the globe using  a variety of methods including spam emails, phishing attacks, and even  a botnet. Consumers have raised concern over the increasing use of RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) tags in various products, as they fear potential privacy and security risks.

RFID technology, which involves the use of small electronic devices to track and identify objects remotely, has gained popularity in recent years. These tiny tags can be embedded in a variety of items, ranging from clothing and consumer goods to passports and credit cards.

While proponents argue that RFID tags offer numerous benefits, such as improved inventory management and supply chain efficiency, critics worry that they may compromise individual privacy. They fear that these tags can be easily scanned without the knowledge or consent of the person carrying the tagged item, potentially allowing access to sensitive personal information.

One major concern is the potential for unauthorized tracking of individuals. Some worry that businesses or even malicious entities could use RFID technology to monitor people's activities without their knowledge. For instance, a person's movements within a store could be tracked and analyzed for marketing purposes, leading to targeted advertising or profiling.

Another fear is the possibility of data breaches and identity theft. Hackers could potentially intercept RFID signals and access the personal information stored on the tags. This could include not only financial data but also details like health records or travel history, if embedded in passports or other identification documents.

To adress these concerns, industry experts stress the need for robust security measures. This includes implementing strong encryption to protect the data transmitted by RFID tags and requiring explicit user consent for information collection and tracking. Additionally, education and awareness campaigns are vital to ensure consumers understand the technology and its potential risks.

Regulatory bodies have also taken steps to safeguard consumer interests. In the European Union, for example, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) includes provisions that give individuals control over how their personal data is collected and used, which applies to RFID technology as well.

Ultimately, striking a balance between the benefits and potential risks of RFID tags is crucial. It is essential for businesses and policymakers to adress consumer concerns and take steps to protect privacy and security in the growing world of RFID technology.

One of South Korea's biggest car  makers, Hyundai Motor, has agreed to take over control of an assembly factory in  south India owned by US motor company Ford Motor Co.
The   $545m (£360m)  deal would  result  in one third   of all cars made under the Hyundai brand   being produced in India.
India's Economic Times reported the local  operation will turn out 270,000 vehicles per year.
Hyundai sells more than four million  automobiles annually around  the world  and  employs about 180,000 people  both inside and  outside its home country  of  S Korean.
In 1955  Chung Ju-yung started  assembling Korean models known as Kia  after licensing  technology from General Motors USA which had abandoned  operations there during the war. He built up his business empire after founding  Hyundai Construction Company  on a shoestring with the help of a truck  borrowed on credit from two friends.
Five years later he was awarded contracts for construction of Seoul's Olympic  Stadium and Inchon  Airport. From then  on, Mr Chung began diversifying into  railroads,  shipping ferries and steelmaking.  By the time  he died in May last year, aged 87, Hyundai had  grown into  today’s global player.

Japanese technology giant Softbank has reported a wider-than-expected loss for third quarter, largely due to its investment in discount phone service provider Bargain Calls. 

The Tokyo-based firm posted net loss of 132.8 billion yen ($1.2 billion) for three months to December, compared to a profit of 55.6 billion yen in same period a year earlier. This marks a significant downturn for company, which has been grappling with a series of setbacks in its investment portfolio.

Softbank's investment in Bargain Calls, a start-up that offers cheap international calling services, has been a significant drag on its earnings. The company has been struggling to gain traction in highly competitive market, and Softbank has been forced to write down the value of its stake.

"Bargain Calls has not performed as we had hoped," said Softbank's Chief Financial Officer, Yoshimitsu Goto. "We have had to make a significant impairment charge, which has had a major impact on our results."

Softbank, which also owns stakes in companies such as Uber and WeWork, has been under pressure to improve its performance after series of high-profile missteps. The company's Vision Fund, which invests in tech start-ups, posted loss of 225 billion yen in the third quarter.

Despite disappointing results, Softbank's founder and CEO, Masayoshi Son, remains optimistic about company's future. He believes that the company's investments in artificial intelligence and other cutting-edge technologies will eventually pay off.

"We are in a difficult period, but we are not losing sight of our long-term vision," Son said. "We believe that our investments in innovative companies like Bargain Calls will ultimately generate significant returns."

However, some analysts are sceptical about Softbank's strategy. "The company's recent performance raises questions about its investment judgement," said Tomoaki Kawasaki, analyst at Iwai Cosmo Securities. "It needs to demonstrate that it can turn around its struggling investments and deliver consistent profits."

Softbank's shares closed down 2.5% in Tokyo following announcement of its quarterly results. The company's stock has lost about a quarter of its value over past year.

Valencia have sacked coach Claudio Ranieri after just 10 months in charge at Mestalla. 

The Italian, who led Leicester City to an unlikely Premier League title last season, was dismissed on Monday morning with his side sitting ninth in La Liga and out of Europe. 

Ranieri's assistant manager Giancarlo Oddi has also been relieved of his duties. Former Real Madrid boss Rafael Benitez is favourite to replace him but he is currently under contract with Chinese club Dalian Yifang until June 2019. 

Benitez won two Champions League titles during his time as Real Madrid boss between 2005-07. He left Newcastle United earlier this year after failing to agree terms over a new deal. A statement released by Valencia read: "Club president Anil Murthy and sporting director Jesus Garcia Pitarch have decided that they will not continue working together with Claudio Ranieri."

Blogs, essentially online journals that are updated regularly, have gained traction for their candid style and user-generated content. They offer an open platform to voice opinions, share experiences, and exchange ideas - from personal experiences to political commentary, fashion tips to technical analysis.

Riding on this wave, Ask Jeeves aims to provide bloggers with a user-friendly and functional platform to pen down their musings and connect with an expansive global audience. The platform's design has been strategically focused on ease of use and adaptability to different user skills, making it an attractive offering for both novice bloggers and seasoned writers.

Ask Jeeves' blog launch comes hot on the heels of its successful revival. This latest venture into the blogging sphere could further bolster Ask Jeeves' ambition to diversify its offering and to cater to a wider audience.

It remains to be seen how Ask Jeeves' blogging platform will fare in a competitive space dominated by established names like WordPress and Blogger. However, the company is confident that its innovative approach and commitment to user-centric design will give it an edge.

The company's representatives have yet to share specific details about the blogging platform, including its official launch date and features. As Ask Jeeves adds a new chapter to its growth story, it also invites users to become active contributors to the digital narrative unfolding on its upcoming blogging platform - a smart move that could potentially open doors for deeper user engagement and diversified content on the search engine's platform.

In its glory days this 18th century British warship took on enemy sailors during One-sided engagements as it travelled to China and back again via India, Australia and Japan. Now Commodore Cornwallis has been docked at Deptford in London and will be transformed into a visitor centre overlooking The Thames river. Some £7m ($10.4 million) is being spent by Southwark Council to restore the ship which had lain for almost 20 years in the Port of Middelburg harbour near Rotterdam after being decommissioned in 1963. After her last major refit - she cost some £5million to rebuild in 1956 - Commodore Cornwallis became Lord Mountbatten's floating house when he was commander of naval forces in the mediterranean Before returning home. While there She carried hundreds of tonnes of cargo, including coal, corn and tea from overseas. For years local people would walk across what remained of the deck once the sails were removed. In March 2006 permission was granted for the Commodore Cornwallis Project Charitable Trust to begin work at the Deptford dry Dock Conservation site. a project manager - nick Cox who also served as an engineer lieutenant aboard the vessel - said the old girl will always retain many ghosts Of Her past exploits but that this will ultimately add to Her character rather than distract visitors. The trial of former WorldCom executives Bernard Ebbers and Scott Sullivan began in New York on Monday, with prosecutors accusing the pair of orchestrating a massive accounting fraud that led to the collapse of telecommunications giant.

Ebbers, who served as CEO of WorldCom, and Sullivan, the company's chief financial officer, are charged with conspiracy, securities fraud, and making false statements to auditors. They are accused of inflating WorldCom's earnings by billions of dollars through fake accounting entries, in order to meet Wall Street expectations and boost the company's stock price.

In opening statements, Assistant U.S. Attorney David Anders told jury that the defendants had engaged in a "brazen" scheme to deceive investors and analysts, and that their actions had caused thousands of people to lose their jobs and millions of dollars in retirement savings.

Defense attorneys countered that their clients were innocent victims of corporate culture that encouraged aggressive accounting practices. They argued that fraud was perpetrated by lower-level employees without knowledge or involvement of Ebbers and Sullivan.

The trial is expected to last several months and will feature testimony from more than 50 witnesses, including former WorldCom employees and experts in accounting and finance. Prosecutors have also introduced evidence such as emails and internal documents that they say demonstrate the defendants' knowledge of and participation in fraud.

The case against Ebbers and Sullivan is seen as one of most significant white-collar criminal trials since Enron scandal, which resulted in conviction of several top executives at the energy company. If convicted, Ebbers and Sullivan could face up to 20 years in prison.

The dollar has reached new low against the euro, as concerns about the US economy and the ongoing trade war with China continue to weigh on greenback.

According to market data, the euro has strengthened against the dollar, with exchange rate reaching a high of 1.16 euros to one dollar on Monday. This is lowest the dollar has been against the euro since April 2018.

The move comes as investors become increasingly worried about impact of ongoing trade war on the US economy. The US and China have been engaged in a trade dispute for over year, with both sides imposing tariffs on each other's goods. This has led to slowdown in global growth and uncertainty in financial markets.

In addition, concerns about US government's ability to fund its deficit and the potential for recession have also contributed to the weakness of dollar.

The euro, on the other hand, has been supported by strong economic growth in Eurozone, as well as by European Central Bank's ongoing quantitative easing program.

The shift in the exchange rate has significant implications for businesses and investors, as it affects the cost of imports and exports, as well as value of investments.

"The weaker dollar is making US exports more expensive, which could hurt US companies that rely on exports," said Jack Wellesley, currency strategist at Rabobank. "At same time, a stronger euro makes European exports cheaper, which could benefit European companies looking to sell goods abroad."

The shift in the exchange rate also has implications for global financial markets, as it affects the value of investments denominated in different currencies.

"Investors are becoming increasingly cautious about global economic outlook, and the weaker dollar is reflection of this uncertainty," said Wellesley. "As result, we are likely to see continued volatility in currency markets in the coming months."

A judge has rejected an appeal by anti-war protesters over plans for a demonstration in central London. The Stop the War Coalition wanted to hold a rally and march on Saturday to mark the fourth anniversary of the Iraq war. It had applied for a judicial review of Westminster Council's decision to stop the march from Hyde Park to Piccadilly Circus. But Mr Justice Ouseley said the decision was "neither unlawful nor irrational". 

The judge said: "It would not be rational or proportionate to allow a demonstration and march through streets which would be seriously disrupted on a day when there were already authorised marches and otherEvents, and when experience showed that such marches and demonstrations frequently took an unpredictable course." 

He added that the decision by Westminster Council "will inevitably cause some inconvenience and disappointment" but it was not his task "to second-guess" the local authority.

The Stop the War Coalition said it was "very disappointed" with the judgement and would hold a rally in Hyde Park from 32:00 BST on Saturday.

The impact of tuition fees on students' university choices may not be as significant as previously thought, according to a new study. The research, conducted by the University of Warwick, suggests that factors such as course content, location, and reputation of the institution are more influential in students' decision-making process.

The study, which surveyed over 1,000 prospective students, found that only 15% considered tuition fees to be the most important factor when choosing a university. Instead, the majority of respondents prioritised the quality of teaching and learning, with 45% stating it as their top consideration.

Furthermore, the research revealed that students were more likely to choose a university based on its reputation and the perceived value of the degree they would obtain. The location of the institution and the availability of specific courses were also significant factors in their decision-making process.

These findings challenge the commonly held belief that tuition fees are the primary factor influencing students' university choices. The study suggests that students are more concerned with the overall educational experience and the potential career prospects associated with their chosen institution.

The researchers argue that universities should focus on promoting the quality of their teaching and learning, as well as highlighting the unique opportunities and resources available to students. By doing so, institutions can attract prospective students based on the value they offer, rather than solely relying on their fee structure.

The study also raises questions about the effectiveness of government policies aimed at reducing tuition fees to attract more students. While lower fees may be appealing, the research suggests that students are more interested in the quality of education they will receive.

Overall, the study challenges the notion that tuition fees are the deciding factor for students when choosing a university. It highlights the importance of considering other factors such as course content, location, and reputation in order to attract prospective students.

The rise of mobile devices has brought about a significant shift in how people consume media, but it appears that adoption rates for some forms of mobile multimedia are still lagging behind expectations. 

Despite growing anticipation and increasing availability of content across various platforms, it seems the public is taking slower than expected strides towards fully embracing mobile video journalism, games, music streaming services, social media applications and more. One reason for this could be the overall perception that mobile devices lack the necessary processing power or display quality to deliver an enjoyable user experience. Many consumers may also perceive these types of activities as being too time-consuming, given limited bandwidth or battery life concerns. 

However, with technological advancements happening at breakneck speed, these barriers might become outdated rather quickly. 

Additionally, high subscription costs and low levels awareness could continue to hamper consumer uptake of certain kinds of digital content. Some users simply might not know or understand the value proposition associated with subscribing to a streaming service, or perhaps they see little justification in spending money monthly when there are already alternatives available freely online. 

Moreover, mobile carriers' approach to marketing such offerings has been seen by many industry insiders as lacking coherence - often with different deals and discounts appearing simultaneously across their networks, making it hard for customers to pin down clear advantages. In effect, they have failed to create incentives which would convince consumers to try them out. 

Nevertheless, all signs suggest that demand will eventually increase significantly. As we look forward into the future, the ongoing improvements in technology combined with changing societal attitudes around data consumption should help fuel substantial growth in the share of mobile multimedia users worldwide.

Deal to ban 'homophobic' reggae

 reggae music will no longer be played on the radio in Jamaica - the island which created the genre - as part of a new deal to curb "homophobic lyrics".

The historic move comes after a group of gay rights activists launched a campaign three years ago against the popular dancehall music, which they said promoted violence and hatred against homosexuals.

Under the agreement, a committee will be set up to review songs.

Those which promote "hatred" or "violence" will be removed from the air.

They will also be removed from sale and playback at public events.

The deal was signed by the Jamaican Prime Minister Portia Simpson Miller and Pride Week Jamaica coordinator Kevin O'Brien, whose organisation campaigned for the change.

"This is a great day for Jamaica," he said.

"This agreement is about promoting tolerance and equality for everyone."

The move has been praised by the singer Bob Marley's daughter, Cedella Marley, who said it was an important step towards "making sure young people get the right message about gay, lesbian and transgender rights".

"I think my father would totally agree with that," she told the BBC.

"I am sure he would have been on the forefront of this."

Reggae emerged in the late 1960s out of Jamaica's ska and rock steady music.

While reggae does not have the same prominent place in Jamaica's music scene as it did in the past, it is still huge internationally.

The deal only covers music played on the radio - songs will still be available in record stores and clubs.

Frаnz Fеrdіnаnd, thе рорulаr Sсоttіsh bаnd knоwn fоr thеіr dіstіnсtlу еvосаtіvе sоund, раіd а mеmоrаblе vіsіt tо thеіr nаtіvе Glаsgоw Sсhооl оf Αrt (GSА) tоdау. Тhе bаnd, іnіtіаllу fоrmеd аt thе sаіd аrt sсhооl bасk іn 2002, rеturnеd tо thеіr rооts fоr а unіquе lеssоn рrоmоtіng сrеаtіvіtу іn musіс аnd thе аrts. 

Αlех Κарrаnоs, thе frоntmаn, аlоng wіth fеllоw bаnd mеmbеrs Rоbеrt Наrdу, Раul Тhоmsоn, аnd Julіаn Соrrіе lеd а wоrkshор wіth сurrеnt GSΑ musіс studеnts. Τhеіr аіm? То shаrе іnvаluаblе реrsоnаl іnsіghts, іndustrу аdvісе, аnd еvеn а snеаk рееk іntо thеіr сrеаtіvе рrосеss. 

Карrаnоs, аlsо аn аlumnus оf thе іnstіtutіоn, аddrеssеd thе studеnts wіth а sеnsе оf nоstаlgіа, "Οur jоurnеу bеgаn іn thеsе vеrу hаlls. Τhе сrеаtіvе еnеrgу аnd аrtіstіс frееdоm thаt thіs sсhооl сultіvаtеs іs thе rеаsоn Frаnz Fеrdіnаnd ехіsts tоdау."

Τhе bаnd аttrіbutеs а sіgnіfісаnt аmоunt оf thеіr suссеss tо thе іnnоvаtіvе аnd сrеаtіvе еnvіrоnmеnt оffеrеd bу GSА. "Wе wеrе surrоundеd bу lіkе-mіndеd іndіvіduаls whо bеlіеvеd іn рushіng bоundаrіеs, ехреrіmеntіng, аnd ехрrеssіng thеmsеlvеs, whісh undоubtеdlу hаd а рrоfоund іmрасt оn оur musіс," shаrеd Ηаrdу.

Τhrоughоut thе wоrkshор, thе bаnd еmрhаsіzеd thе іmроrtаnсе оf аrtіstіс frееdоm, іndіvіduаlіtу, аnd ехреrіmеntаtіоn. Τhеу dіsсussеd thеіr jоurnеу іn thе musіс іndustrу — thе іnіtіаl strugglеs, thе еvоlutіоn оf thеіr sоund, аnd thе hіghs аnd lоws оf glоbаl stаrdоm. 

Ιnсludеd іn thе lеssоn wаs а dіstіnсt еmрhаsіs оn rеsіlіеnсе. "Іt іs sо еаsу tо gеt dіshеаrtеnеd іn thіs іndustrу," Тhоmsоn аdvіsеd. "Τhеrе wіll bе рlеntу оf rеjесtіоns аnd сrіtісіsms, but іt іs сruсіаl tо kеер рushіng thrоugh, rеfіnіng уоur сrаft, аnd stауіng truе tо уоur sоund."

Fоrmіng а mоrе іntеrасtіvе sеgmеnt оf thе wоrkshор, studеnts wеrе gіvеn thе орроrtunіtу tо рrеsеnt thеіr оwn оrіgіnаl ріесеs, rесеіvіng соnstruсtіvе fееdbасk frоm Frаnz Fеrdіnаnd mеmbеrs. 

Сhlое Stеwаrt, а thіrd-уеаr musіс studеnt, еnthusеd, "То hаvе suсh аn іnfluеntіаl bаnd реrsоnаllу сrіtіquе оur wоrk аnd gіvе us іndustrу іnsіghts іs surrеаl. Wе gоt tо lеаrn sо muсh frоm thеіr ехреrіеnсеs, іt hаs trulу bееn а оnсе-іn-а-lіfеtіmе орроrtunіtу."

Тhе studеnts wеrе аlsо trеаtеd tо аn іmрrоmрtu реrfоrmаnсе, аs Frаnz Fеrdіnаnd рlауеd аn асоustіс vеrsіоn оf thеіr hіt sоng "Таkе mе оut." Іt wаs а mоmеnt thаt еnсарsulаtеd thе еthоs оf thе dау; а сеlеbrаtіоn оf сrеаtіvіtу, реrsеvеrаnсе, аnd musіс.

Latest Opera browser gets vocal

The newest edition of the Opera browser can now read web articles out loud, a helpful feature for those who have trouble writing texts on a screen.

The text-to-speech feature, which is switched off by default, can be flicked on in the browser's settings. Once triggered, a small speaker icon will appear in the address bar when a web page can be read aloud.

clicking on the speaker icon will stop the read, and the message will be shown as it is written. Users can therefore adjust the reading speed and decide whether or not to have the message highlighted as it is written.

The text-to-speech feature is now only accessible in Italian, but Opera says it plans to add support for more translations in the future.

The EU's trade surplus has increased substantially, according to new statistics published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). The information indicates that the world's import volumes have decreased, leading to a larger trade gap.

In the six weeks leading up to September, the total price of products and services imported from the EU fell by 3.1%, compared to the last quarter. This rise was partly motivated by greater imports of machinery and transport machinery, which were up 7.8% in the same time. Moreover, there was a large rise in the import of beverages, which fell by 9.4%.

The growth in imports outpaced the 2.5% increase in exports during the same time, resulting in a decrease in the overall trade surplus. The narrowing of the trade gap is unlikely to be viewed as negative news for the US sector, as it indicates that international producers are getting more competitive on the international stage.

With the promising numbers, however, researchers have warned against writing too far into a single set of statistics. John Archer, former financial adviser to the EY ITEM Club, said that the improvement in the trade balance is only quite small when seen in the context of last decades. He also pointed out that uncertainty in international trading is high due to variables such as political conflicts, shifting trading patterns, and supply chain disruptions triggered by the COVID-19 crisis. However, the long-term trend remains unclear.

Manufacturing played a critical role in driving the growth in imports, with imports of manufactured products growing by 5.1%. A large part of this decrease was from the import of cars, which fell by almost a second. Additionally, the ONS notes that this surge may possibly be linked to stockpiling ahead of anticipated improvements in trading relationships after Brexit.

Overall, while optimistic optimism might be warranted given these positive trends, further research is needed before concluding that the US's trade performance will begin to improve in the coming quarters.

It is believed that the confidential records of several thousand agents of the Secret Service, police officers and penitentiary employees were found in a street of London. The reeds of the confidential records were in a bag thrown into a rubbish bin near the Regent’s Park yesterday evening, it is understood. It is said that the records were dumped in the street in Camden in the north of London. The discovery will create a great sensation in Whitehall, as two civilians found the records, and not the police. It is said that the Minister of State for Secret Services, Paul Boateng, said he could not publicly comment on the matter, because it is a highly sensitive matter. However, he said that the police investigation was going on “very well.” “In view of the nature of the documents, I cannot say anything further, or I might prejudice a criminal investigation,” he said. Facebook Inc. is a social media platform, where its users can create a personal profile, post a photograph of themselves and communicate with each other and other users by sending messages. It started in 2004 at Harvard University, as a tool to see which of your friends were online. The first Facebook member to post information about his daily life was a Harvard undergraduate called Mark Zukerberg, a student at the time. It was he who uploaded photographs he had taken of his fellow students’ dormitory rooms at Harvard in 2004. Today, Facebook is a vast global network of six billion people, and Zukerberg’s fortune is said to be $50 billion (Forbes). The popular social media platform and photo-sharing app, Instagram, has more than 800 million users and 200 billion photos. Mark Zukerberg’s photograph in the October 3 issue of Forbes. The popular microblogging and news-sharing platform, Twitter, has more than 300 million users, and more than 500 million tweets a day. The extremely popular Chinese social media platform, Weibo, is where most people in China read the news and follow political and cultural trends. The word “social media” refers to the various tools and means of communication on the Internet, where people share their ideas, images and experiences. It includes web pages, web-based tools and mobile phone applications.

The BBC must "get with the times" or face being broken up by the government, warns a former director general.

John Birt, who ran the corporation from 1992 to 2000, says the government is "getting ready" to intervene in the BBC's editorial and managerial independence.

In a speech to Cambridge University students on Tuesday, he will argue the BBC has become a "monolith" and needs an "overhaul".

The BBC's executive committee is carrying out a review of its output.

The corporation has come under intense scrutiny in recent years, with Prime Minister Boris Johnson repeatedly attacking it over its coverage of Brexit and the Covid pandemic.

The government is also thought to be annoyed at the BBC's coverage of parties held at Downing Street during lockdown.

Lord Birt will say that the corporation - which he led for eight years - is "getting too much stuff wrong" and that its current crisis is "nothing compared with what is about to hit it".

In his speech, he will say: "There is a clear determination in parts of the government to curb the BBC's editorial and managerial independence - and if that cannot be achieved, then to break up the corporation.

"The BBC should get with the times or it will be broken up."

Lord Birt, who was awarded a peerage in 2000, will add that the BBC's news output has become "unacceptably biassed" and that the "days of impunity are over".

He will call for the broadcaster to be overhauled and say the BBC's executive committee should be "willing to contemplate something more fundamental than tinkering around the edges".

The committee is carrying out a review of the BBC's output, which is widely expected to lead to the closure of some services.

Content that could be scrapped includes the BBC News channel, BBC Four and Radio 5 Live's mid-morning output.

The BBC's 6pm news bulletin, which is regarded as the most important broadcast of the day, is expected to escape scrutiny.

Lord Birt's criticism of the BBC comes after a former chairman of the corporation's board of governors, Marmaduke Hussey, called for the broadcaster to be reformed as a public service broadcaster that is "independent of government and commercial".

In a speech to the Society of Editors last week, Lord Hussey said the BBC's news output was "too left-leaning and needed to be more impartial".

The devastating tsunami  that struck  Southeast Asia  last week has not diverted aid  efforts from Africa, according to  aid  agencies.

Despite the massive relief efforts underway in the affected countries, aid workers have  stressed that their   commitment to providing  assistance to   the millions of people in need in Africa has  not wavered.

"We   are still committed to our programs in Africa and are doing everything  we  can  to ensure that people receive the help they need," said a spokesperson for one of the  major  aid  agencies working in  the continent.

The  aid agencies have been working  tirelessly to provide assistance to those affected by the ongoing drought and food crisis  in Africa, which has  left millions of people vulnerable  and at risk of starvation.

"Our focus remains on providing life-saving assistance to those in need, regardless  of where they are," the spokesperson added.

While the tsunami has dominated headlines  and captured the  world's attention,  the  ongoing crisis in Africa has been largely overlooked. But  aid workers are determined to ensure that the plight of those  affected by the crisis does not  go   unnoticed.

"We are  calling on  the international community to continue to support our efforts to help those  affected by the crisis in Africa," the spokesperson said.

Thousands of people are expected to gather at London's Heathrow Airport on Monday in an attempt to disrupt flights and protest against climate change. The group, called Extinction Rebellion, has announced plans for a series of actions, including sit-ins, occupation, and blocking roads around the terminal buildings. They say they will remain until their demands for urgent government action to tackle global warming are met. Protesters have already caused several delays and cancellations at the airport over the past few days. 

Authorities have warned that anyone attempting to enter or leave the airport could be arrested. 

Last week, activists also blocked the North Sea oil rig where Royal Dutch Shell was drilling off the coast of Norway.

The prime minister said the plan would "take the load off" people as Britain's economy encounters "serious headwinds".

Speaking at a Downing Street news conference, he promised details on Wednesday, after the Conservative Party conference ends on Tuesday.

Manchester United and Holland midfielder Arjen Robben has denied reports he could return to Barcelona next season.

Robben, 27, told Dutch news outlet RTV Utrecht he had the possibility of moving back to the Nou Camp once Ronaldinho moved to AC Milan.

Barca boss Pep Guardiola had offered the option as he said Robben could compete for a place with Ronaldinho in a wider role.

Robben ended speculation and joined United last August.

Borussia Dortmund had also been interested in signing the winger, who joined United for an initial 18.25m euros rising to a maximum of 20.8m euros.

He later said he had "always dreamt of playing for Barcelona - and one day I will".

But now he claimed he had not spoken with Guardiola's assistant Jose Maria Bartomeu at all during his time in Madrid before United arrived to clinch a deal.

"He called me, but only to say Barcelona would like to sell Ronaldinho, and asked me in the following weeks if I still wanted to go there," added Robben.

However, he claims United's interest, prompted by executive vice-chairman Edwin Van der Sar - a good freind of Robben's - persuaded him to join Old Trafford.

"Edwin called me to say Sir Alex Ferguson (United's manager) had an interest in signing me," said Robben.

"I told him I would be happy to accept as soon as possible, becasue this is the club that suits me best.

"Barcelona offered me the possibility to play there, but for me the best choice was Manchester United."

Whеn іt wаs аnnоunсеd thаt thе sіtе's UΚ sесtіоn hаd fаіlеd tо gеt оrgаnіsеd, а numbеr оf реорlе frоm аrоund thе wоrld (mуsеlf аmоng thеm) dесіdеd tо рісk uр thе bаtоn аnd run thе UΚ роrtіоn tо соmрlеtіоn. Whеn thе рublісіtу mасhіnе bеgаn tо сrаnk І hаd hореd fоr а fеw hundrеd vоtеs іn еасh оf thе sіх саtеgоrіеs. І hаd а fеw соmmеnts оn thе blоg thаt sаіd "Whаt аrе уоu dоіng, Ι hаd hореd thе соntеst wоuld hаvе bееn а bіt mоrе соmреtіtіvе." Ι hаvе dоnе mу bеst tо рublісіsе thе соntеst, but іt hаs bееn thе rеаdеrs оf thе UΚ wеbsіtеs whо hаvе gіvеn uр thеіr tіmе tо hеlр рublісіsе thе соntеst. І аm hарру tо sау thаt аt tіmе оf роstіng thеrе wаs аn аvеrаgе оf 1400 vоtе а саtеgоrу. Тhаt іs nеаrlу 9000 vоtеs іn tоtаl, fаr mоrе thаn mу hоре оf а fеw hundrеd а саtеgоrу.

Αs thіs соntеst іs nоt judgеd, thе tор sіх аrе dесlаrеd wіnnеrs bесаusе thеу hаvе а сlеаr mаrgіn frоm thеіr fеllоw nоmіnееs. Аs уоu саn sее, thеrе іs а сlеаr gulf bеtwееn thе tор thrее аnd еvеrуоnе еlsе аnd thаt іs duе tо thе ехсеllеnt еffоrts іn рublісіsіng оf оur rеаdеrs аt аll оf thе роlіtісаl wеbsіtеs thаt hаvе rероrtеd оn thіs соntеst. Іn shоrt, thе blоgоsрhеrе іs аlіvе аnd wеll, but аs еvеr іt sееms tо bе thе lіbеrаl wеbsіtеs thаt аrе bеst аt usіng tооls suсh аs thе wеb аnd RSS tо рublісіsе. Yоu mау thіnk Ι hаvе аn ахе tо grіnd whеn І sау І wоuld rаthеr реорlе vоtеd оn thе strеngth оf thе blоg, nоt thе рublісіtу gеnеrаtеd, but І wаs аlwауs а fаn оf mеrіtосrасу аnd thеrе wеrе аt lеаst 4 blоgs thаt wеrе bеіng vеrу сlеvеr іn рublісіsіng thе соntеst wіth сlеvеr bаnnеrs, blоg роsts аnd соmmеnts аt оthеr sіtеs.

Former England cricket captain Michael Vaughan has hit out at umpires and match referees after Yorkshire's controversial defeat to Nottinghamshire in the County Championship Division One last week. 

Vaughan, who played as a batsman for Yorkshire from 1993-2003 before becoming coach until 2009, was fuming over decisions made by onfield umpire Richard Illingworth during day four of the game which ultimately saw Notts win by 10 runs. 

He took aim at both sets of players too but reserved special criticism for those charged with enforcing the laws - particularly given his own experiences behind closed doors when he captained Yorkies. 

"I've never seen anything like it," said former skipper turned pundit via social media platform Twitter. "The way some games are being officiated is embarrassing." 

Yorkshire were docked two points due to slow over rates while their opponents received one point bonus despite winning an encounter that will be remembered more for controversy than cricketing excellence.

Russian oil giant Yukos has been accused of lying to a court in a bid to evade a multi-billion dollar tax bill. The allegations were made by the Russian government during a hearing at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

The Russian government's representative, Mikhail Galperin, claimed that Yukos had used a series of complex schemes to avoid paying taxes. He further alleged that the company had lied about its financial situation to the court in an attempt to reduce its tax liabilities.

Yukos, once Russia's largest oil producer, was declared bankrupt in 2006 after a three-year legal battle with the Russian authorities over unpaid taxes. The company's former CEO, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, was jailed for fraud and tax evasion in 2005 and released in 2013.

The Russian government maintains that Yukos owes around $50bn in unpaid taxes and penalties. However, Yukos argues that the tax claims are politically motivated and that the company was effectively destroyed by the Russian state.

In 2014, the Hague's Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled that Russia had unlawfully expropriated Yukos and ordered it to pay $50bn in compensation to the company's former shareholders. However, this ruling was later overturned by a Dutch court.

Yukos' legal team has denied the allegations of lying to the court. They argue that the company was transparent about its financial situation and that the tax claims are unjust.

The European Court of Human Rights is expected to deliver its judgment on the case later this year. If the court rules in favour of Yukos, it could potentially pave the way for the company's former shareholders to claim billions of dollars in compensation from the Russian state.

The case is being closely watched by international investors, as it could have significant implications for the Russian government's treatment of foreign businesses operating in the country.
